We delve into the case of del Pezzo surfaces, establishing a precise relationship between their mutation classes and Fano surfaces of maximal rank. This relationship enables us to classify all Fano surfaces of maximal rank through the classification of mutation classes of Laurent polynomials corresponding to del Pezzo surfaces of maximal rank, and further, it allows us to classify all mutation classes of Laurent polynomials corresponding to del Pezzo surfaces of maximal rank through the classification of Fano surfaces of maximal rank. Furthermore, we establish that the tropical moduli space of Fano surfaces of maximal rank is isomorphic to the Q-tropical moduli space of mutation classes of Laurent polynomials of toppling degree 8, and this is achieved by introducing a new graph invariant called toppling degree. Additionally, we propose that the tropical moduli space of Fano surfaces of maximal rank can be extended to include Fano surfaces of rank greater than one by defining a new parameter called the tropical rank. It is claimed that the tropical moduli space of Fano surfaces of rank greater than one is isomorphic to the Q-tropical moduli space of mutation classes of Laurent polynomials with tropical rank greater than one. It is also proposed that the tropical rank can be interpreted as the Euler characteristic of the surface's tropicalization and that it has the potential to provide a more comprehensive framework for classifying Fano varieties through their tropical structures. It is noted that the concepts introduced in this work have the potential to contribute positively to the development of higher-dimensional Fano variety classifications. A single face image can generate a range of faces from the same individual through morphing. However, capturing this process analytically is challenging due to the infinite possibilities, thus requiring a learned model. In contrast to recent work that focuses on constructing a face from pose-dependent and independent factors, this paper introduces the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) which simultaneously processes both factors to build a face from two input images, one representing a face in another's eyes and the other in the same person's eyes. By doing so, the model naturally achieves robustness to varying pose dependencies. Through extensive experiments, SADRNet demonstrated superior performance on both synthetic and real-world data in multiple evaluation metrics, ultimately surpassing state-of-the-art methods according to mean absolute error and mean squared error standards. Furthermore, our model successfully decomposed a face into its factor components, demonstrating alignment and separation capabilities. Ultimately, SADRNet successfully constructed a face from two images, one in another's eyes and the other in the same person's eyes, achieving a breakthrough in the field. All of our code and data will be made available on the SADRNet project page. Our paper has also been selected as the oral presentation for the CVPR 2020 conference.

We investigate the electronic properties of fracton matter under the presence of a finite charge density. By employing a doped version of the $A_{3}C_{60}$ structure, we develop a theoretical model that suggests charged fractons may be mobilized within a two-dimensional tubular framework. However, we find that a finite charge density significantly impacts the mobility of fractons by creating a complex potential that affects their motion in a nonlinear manner. As a result, the fracton spectrum becomes highly dispersive, and we are able to derive an effective mass parameter that describes the density's constricting effect on fracton mobility. Based on this understanding, we propose that the effective mass of fractons could be adjusted to align with different quantum points in the Fermi landscape. By doing so, we simulate the implementation of topological charge brackets proposed within quantum computation, leveraging the motion of fractons as a fundamental logical operation. The proposed scheme offers a new perspective on the interpretation of quantum computation, offering possibilities for innovation in the field. Furthermore, we suggest that the principles underlying the physics of fracton matter could be applied to design new quantum phases of matter. Additionally, we explore the possibility of integrating fracton-like particles into photoonic systems, and discuss potential applications for such systems. Finally, we propose that the unique physics of fracton-like particles could be investigated through experiments involving lattice vibrations in doped $A_{3}C_{60}$, and that such studies may reveal additional insights into the properties of these systems.

We introduce a novel framework for analyzing high-dimensional linear models that incorporate infinite-dimensional data, ensuring the model's parameters remain coherent and manageable. We apply this framework to a specific scenario: a traditional linear regression model is expanded to account for time-dependent variables, where the model's parameters are represented as smooth functions of time. By leveraging the framework, we establish an optimal regularization method, L1-band-regularized ODE, to solve this complex model. The L1-band-regularized ODE method successfully tackles the infinite-dimensional data issue by employing the framework's tools, such as the L1 norm for reducing dimensions and the bilinear form for integrating the dynamics. Through theoretical analysis and computational experiments, we demonstrate that this method yields an accurate and efficient estimator. Notably, the L1-band-regularized ODE method can be viewed as an extension of the L1-ODE method to partial linear models, addressing a common generalization challenge. We further illustrate the method's effectiveness by applying it to a synthetic dataset resembling an EEG signal and demonstrate its performance superiority over traditional methods. Moreover, we highlight the L1-band-regularized ODE method's potential to handle diverse time-dependent variables, such as those encountered in EEG signals, by interpreting the estimated parameters with a source localization problem. We conclude that the L1-band-regularized ODE method presents an innovative approach to analyzing time-dependent linear models, extending the scope for the model's parameters and enabling the incorporation of infinite-dimensional data. Additionally, this method offers a compelling solution to the generalization challenge of the L1-ODE method. We anticipate that this method will prove valuable in its own right and also contribute to advancing the L1-ODE method as a practical solution for traditional linear models. We are eager to explore the L1-band-regularized ODE method in relation to other dynamic linear models, such as partial linear panel models, where the parameters are represented as functions of time, but with a focus on a different dynamic system. We believe that this new approach has the potential to address various challenges in high-dimensional statistical analysis, particularly when faced with complex time-dependent variables and infinite-dimensional data. As the transition to a low-carbon economy gathers pace, renewal energies are rising to prominence. However, their intermittent nature demands greater use of energy storage, which must be managed with varying risks in mind. To develop a suitable storage management system, we classify risk-averse storage resources as either risk-averse or risk-prone based on their reaction to the probability of power deficits. The probability threshold that influences their operation serves as a key factor. We argue that a significant proportion of these resources fall into the risk-averse category and operate inflexibly due to existing constraints, which can lead to missed opportunity costs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that optimizing storage deployment under uncertainty can be an complex NP-hard problem. To address this challenge, we developed and tested a simple yet effective heuristic storage deployment algorithm, which considers time-varying renewal energy generation, probability thresholds, and operation costs to determine the optimal storage size and deployment schedule. We applied this algorithm to a simulated UK power system and found that it can reduce storage costs by up to 70% compared to conventional approaches. The success of this algorithm highlights the potential for more flexible storage management and encourages further research into optimizing storage deployment. By comparing experiment and theory, we found that an appropriate choice of photon energy is crucial in achieving coherent core-state excitation. If the energy of the x-ray pulse matches an excited core-state, a particular state can be isolated and excited coherently. However, if the photon energy is too low, the system excites multiple core-states, while using a higher photon energy may lead to excitation of valence-electrons instead. Additionally, we observed that at x-ray energies closer to the core-excitation energy, the core-excited state excited by multiple-electron effects, may lead to different excitation pathways. We created a simplified model of a Martian atmosphere, similar in scale to Earth's, and found that by increasing the ratio of Earth-like characteristics to Martian ones, the baroclinic storms would resemble those found on Mars. Our findings show that for ratios greater than about 0.01, the storms become similar to Mars' dust storm patterns, while for lower ratios, they resemble the circular features seen on Mars. Furthermore, when we increased the atmosphere's stability, the storms on both planets shared more similarities with each other. With this, we were able to apply our model to predict how the Martian atmosphere would behave during episodes of extreme baroclinic storm activity, such as the recent Great Southern Cloud. Current active learning methodologies often assume ideal conditions, where labeled data is obtained exactly as requested, but this assumption falls short in reality due to the limitations of visual detection algorithms used for selection. Our research reveals that these methods fail to account for errors in selecting images, particularly when working with large datasets like ImageNet. We propose a new framework based on Bayesian methods that addresses these challenges and provides accurate results when tested on smaller benchmark datasets, such as CIFAR-10 and MNIST, as well as the larger ImageNet dataset. Our approach involves treating the process of selecting images using a detection algorithm as a non-inclusive, noisy process, where the overlap between the predicted class and the actual class is considered. We demonstrate that this approach yields significantly better performance compared to traditional active learning strategies on both smaller and larger datasets. Our framework's performance is not only superior to existing active learning methods but also robust to various detection algorithms, such as AlexNet, VGG, and DeconvNet, making it a reliable solution for selecting effective images for labeling. We have made our code and data available online for reference.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking multi-agent system that addresses a critical challenge in artificial intelligence - the trust issue. When internet users share their personal data with unknown companies, they often express distrust due to historical data breaches. As a result, these companies find it difficult to engage users in data sharing. Our proposed system, centered on a multi-agent framework, addresses this trust concern. It encourages cooperation among users by facilitating them to share data, which in turn helps in deploying high-accuracy machine learning models instead of conventional methods that compromise on accuracy for limited data. Furthermore, our system ensures enhanced accuracy and trust score in machine learning models by leveraging the power of multiple machine learning algorithms and a consensus-building process between agents. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our system through a case study involving a web application for sharing culinary culture. Experimental results show that our system achieves superior performance, combining the capabilities of multiple deep learning models while maintaining trustworthiness. In particular, our system achieves outstanding results on the CIFAR-10 image classification task, achieving an accuracy of over 80% within just 500 epochs. The remarkable outcomes of our system have significant potential to address trust concerns in big data analytics and deep learning models. The demand for developing reliable and efficient automated lane keeping systems (ALKS) has increased significantly due to increasingly complex and advanced vehicle systems. Accurate and timely testing of ALKS is essential, and this testing process often relies on simulated road networks to evaluate system performance. However, the complexity of modern vehicles requires more sophisticated testing, involving challenging road segments that include transitions, to effectively assess an ALKS's ability to navigate smoothly and safely. In response, we've developed a generative model called FMHN-GAN, utilizing a combination of functional map networks and Gaussian anisotropic product Gaussian processes, to create realistic and complex road networks from simple input descriptions. This model is designed to produce high-quality outputs when trained on limited data, and when trained further, it can generate even more sophisticated scenarios. We demonstrate FMHN-GAN's performance by comparing it to two reference scenarios and validating its safety and performance in various challenging environments. Additionally, we've incorporated FMHN-GAN into a testing framework for ALKS, and conducted multiple experiments to show its effectiveness. Our proposed approach provides a robust solution for generating complex road networks, and the code is available at https://github/FMHN-GAN, offering a useful tool for advancing the development of ALKS.

Recent action proposal networks have achieved high precision but are limited by slow computation. To balance speed and accuracy, we suggest the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), a an an efficient an action proposal network that compensates for limited context by combining visual context from multiple levels. Founded on careful analysis of context aggregation methods, DCAN uses linear transformations to obtain context features of consistent length, thereby boosting performance and compute speed. Through comparison with six alternative context combination methods, we find that standard concatenation produces the fewest context features, but inefficient context use, while adding zero fillers boosts compute speed but diminishes performance. By conventionally standardizing context lengths, DCAN surpasses baseline networks with simultaneous improved performance and compute speed, but is outperformed by faster network variants that prioritize compute speed. The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/cg1174/DCAN.

Currently, evaluating and comparing fuzzers involves measuring delivery rates and effectiveness by testing various time limits. Our research introduces a new evaluation framework that uses modern mutation analysis methods to compare fuzzers. By identifying previously undetected errors in each fuzzer run, our framework provides a more accurate evaluation of fuzzers. To support this approach, we include a new metric called Error Detection Rate (EDR) that measures the percentage of previously undetected errors found by each fuzzer. To minimize biases, we developed a two-stage evaluation process that first measures delivery rates and then ranks fuzzers based on EDR without considering time constraints. To ensure reproducibility and to facilitate future research, we have launched a new website that allows for easy comparison and reproduction of our results. Furthermore, we have introduced a publicly accessible dataset that includes the findings of our evaluation, along with previously developed metrics, to provide a common ground for researchers to compare their results with ours. Our framework and associated tools are now available under an permissive license to facilitate the comparison and evaluation of fuzzers in the field of software testing.

We argue that this indicates the presence of an apparent achievement gap in the evaluation of continual learning methods. 

We suggest closing this gap by conducting more rigorous evaluations of proposed continual learning methods, including comparison to simpler baselines such as the Nearest Mean Classifier. 

We also offer our code and dataset processing tools to the research community to facilitate the development of new continual learning approaches. 

Finally, we discuss potential avenues for advancing the field of continual learning in the context of large-scale datasets using pre-trained models. 

This could potentially involve exploring new evaluation protocols that account for the exceptional performance of baselines in such scenarios.

We conclude by outlining promising directions for further research in this area.

Lipschitz games have been a significant focus in recent years, and our research proposes a generalized version called quasi-Lipschitz games, where each player is assigned a unique Lipschitz value. We demonstrated that quasi-Lipschitz games can be equivalently represented as an assortment of Lipschitz games, comprising distinct subsets of the player set. Furthermore, we established an explicit formula for calculating the optimal strategies in quasi-Lipschitz games by breaking down the component Lipschitz games. Additionally, we developed an efficient computational method for determining the equilibrium payoffs in quasi-Lipschitz games through the use of an assortment of linear programming problems. We validated the genuine generality of our quasi-Lipschitz games framework by showing that both classical Lipschitz games and generalized Lipschitz games can be represented as a subset of quasi-Lipschitz games. Lastly, we highlighted the practical implications and potential applications of our quasi-Lipschitz games framework. Our research is complemented by a comprehensive computational toolset, accessible at https://github.com/yinghuihui/quasi-lipschitz-games, enabling users to compute equilibrium strategies and payoffs for quasi-Lipschitz games through an intuitive graphical interface. This toolset is particularly useful for examining the equilibrium dynamics in quasi-Lipschitz games with continuous player sets. We also introduced a novel method for ranking the strategic value of players based on their assigned Lipschitz values, which provides insights into the relative equilibrium payoffs that players can achieve. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed methods by conducting comprehensive computational experiments and analyzing various real-world scenarios. Lastly, we identified several promising directions for further research in this area. Bucket Elimination (BE) is a highly efficient algorithm for combining various inference and optimization tasks within complex graphical models, often bypassing the need to reconstruct the minimum spanning tree or perform dynamic programming. Despite its advantages, BE's effectiveness is hindered by the laborious calculation of potentials for its buckets. This research introduces an innovative strategy to alleviate this computational burden by exploiting the structure of numerical potentials, a straightforward approach that significantly simplifies the elimination process and facilitates the beaming step. We demonstrate that by reducing the size of buckets, the optimal solution can be obtained without delay, and present guidelines for determining the ideal bucket size based on the available computational resources. Furthermore, our research offers the BE algorithm as a valuable tool for integrating BE with other optimization algorithms, enabling the solution of large-scale problems by dividing them into manageable sub-problems. We showcase the efficacy of our approach by applying it to several real-world problems, including resource allocation, scheduling, and probabilistic modeling, and make all source code publicly available for further development and customization. We also include an efficient implementation of the algorithm in MATLAB, along with exemplary use cases and BE's source code on GitHub for easy access and modification. We hope that this revised version of the algorithm, along with its public source code, will stimulate further innovation and facilitate the adoption of BE as a standard method for combining inference and optimization tasks within complex graphical models. This is particularly relevant when working with large-scale, distributed systems or when facing computational memory constraints. We look forward to contributing to the BE source code and exploring new applications for the algorithm together with the research community. This revised article serves as an updated overview of the BE algorithm, along with our proposed bucket size strategy, and is accompanied by an open-access dataset that includes all source code and exemplar use cases available at https://doi.org/10.17639/2023-02-10. Nonetheless, we believe that the central value decomposition approach presented in this article has the potential to be applied to additional numerical potential types beyond just factors. Moreover, we view this technique as a useful BE algorithm component that can be utilized in conjunction with other optimization algorithms, in order to accelerate the solution processing time for complex graphical models. We hope that this will spark further innovation and facilitate the widespread adoption of the BE algorithm in the field of graphical models. This study examines how the collapse of shipping cartels affected freight rates and shipping volume from 1945 to 1974.  Eleven major shipping routes are analyzed, showing that breaking cartels led to significant increases in freight rates and notable declines in shipping volume.  Our data reveals a complex, non-linear response to the collapse of cartels, with increased freight rates and shipping volume declines in the short-term, followed by more modest freight rate increases and greater shipping volume growth in the long-term.  Furthermore, a substantial portion of the shipping industry's growth during this period can be attributed to the collapse of cartels, as well as the establishment of new shipping routes and the expansion of existing routes.  Additionally, our research finds that shipping routes with shorter durations were more likely to exhibit increased shipping volume growth following the collapse of cartels.  These results provide valuable insights into the behavior of shipping cartels and the effects of anti-trust policies on freight markets.  They also suggest that freight price ceilings, implemented during World War II, contributed to the emergence and persistence of shipping cartels.  Finally, our research suggests that the shipping industry's carrelized structure, combined with price wars and voluntary shipment reductions, can lead to complex, oscillatory equilibria in freight markets.  These findings have important implications for the design of policies aimed at promoting competition in freight markets.  We conclude that a combination of rigorous anti-trust enforcement, targeted policies to address supply chain bottlenecks, and strategic licensing of shipping capacity is necessary to encourage shipping competition and efficient freight pricing.  Our research also offers methodological contributions, leveraging recent advances in econometric methods for analyzing irreversible events in the face of multiple, confounding shocks. This insight suggests that future research on enhancing GNN performance should focus on addressing fundamental limitations of GNNs rather than relying on complex graph structures. Additionally, our analysis highlights the influence of modeling choices on graph structure, revealing that complex graph structures can often be analogous to basic ones and highlighting the need for a clear theoretical definition of graph structure. Our study examines how a cylindrical intruder moves through different types of granular materials under various conditions. We've conducted a comprehensive analysis that combines theoretical and experimental components. Our experimental approach involves observing the motion of a cylindrical intruder passing through various granular materials, including sand, powder, and small spherical beads, at multiple speed increments. In contrast, our theoretical approach is based on a bifurcation model that takes into account the effects of intruder velocity and a critical value known as the jamming threshold. Our findings show that when the intruder's velocity is below the jamming threshold, its motion is determined by a steady-state flow that relies on both the properties of the surrounding material and the intruder itself. However, when the intruder's velocity exceeds the jamming threshold, the surrounding material responds differently to different speed increments, resulting in distinct regimes of motion that correspond to the onset of jamming and a stable flow within the intragerm region. Our research reveals that the drag experienced by the intruder is primarily influenced by the driving rate rather than the type of material it is moving through, ultimately leading to a universal relationship that can be applied across various granular materials. This universal relationship is then used to develop a revised bifurcation model that explains our observed results and provides a framework for further investigation. Our study provides new insights into the complex interaction between an intruder and a granular material and offers a revised theoretical model that can be experimentally validated. Ultimately, our research is a crucial step towards developing a universal framework for understanding the physics underlying the motion of intruders within granular materials. Our work is a crucial precursor to exploring more intricate scenarios, such as the interaction between multiple intruders, by establishing a fundamental universal framework that can be applied across various contexts. Additionally, our study is a necessary foundation for investigating the effects of friction and elasticity on the motion of intruders within granular materials, which will ultimately lead to a deeper understanding of the complex physics underlying these systems. Our work is a vital milestone in our quest to uncover the underlying universal principles that govern the behavior of intruders within granular materials and sets the stage for the exploration of more intricate scenarios. It is also anticipated that our discovered universal relationships will prove applicable to a broader range of contexts, such as the motion of particles in highly viscous fluids. Using high-resolution spectroscopy from HiRES and a model for gas outflows, 
we analyzed the ionized gas outflows in starburst galaxies and how they 
affect gas consumption rates. Our study examined six galaxies undergoing 
rapid star formation and compared them to six normal galaxies. The results 
indicated that gas outflows are common in both starburst and normal galaxies,
with masses up to 1.5 billion times that of the Sun. However, a significant
mass loss was only observed in the starburst galaxies, indicating an energy
budget of around 10 to the power of 56 ergs. We calculated the rate of mass
loss from these outflows and found it to be around 0.3 to the power of 44 
grams per second, which is a small fraction of the total gas consumption 
in these galaxies. Surprisingly, we found that gas consumption rates are 
actually accelerated in galaxies with outflows, by around 10 times. This 
effect is critical for the survival of galaxy islands with outflows, as it 
allows them to counterbalance gas consumption despite losing mass. This 
finds support from observations of gas consumption in nearby galaxies.

while there is a correlation between outflows and supernovae, a massive outflow

boost from another source. We propose a scenario in which outflows are fueled
by the combination of supernovae and an additional source of high-energ
radiation, such as hot gas and active galactic nuclei, which could be the 
beginning of an iterative process that helps consume gas in galaxies.

Our proposed framework, BoAnon, utilizes a learning model that bypasses the necessity for an explicit efficiency metric, allowing it to identify optimal configuration combinations automatically. Unlike conventional approaches, BoAnon eliminates the need for systematic evaluation of configuration options by introducing a novel sampling technique. This innovative method enhances performance by efficiently identifying effective configuration settings without requiring a comprehensive understanding of system internals. As a result, BoAnon accelerates the process of discovering efficient configurations significantly. In evaluation tests, BoAnon demonstrated a speedup of at least 5 times over traditional methods in our experimental settings. Additionally, BoAnon's accuracy was found to be comparable to that of methodical approaches when evaluating the efficacy of configuration combinations. In conclusion, BoAnon offers a viable alternative to traditional methods for identifying efficient configuration settings. This is particularly relevant in context of DDoS mitigation systems, where large numbers of resources necessitate an automated approach to management. Furthermore, BoAnon's learning-based model has the potential to be applied to other complex systems requiring optimal combination of internal resources. This is evident in scenarios such as data center job placement and virtual network design. This framework is currently available online at its corresponding GitHub repository. In future work, BoAnon could be expanded to accommodate time-varying system parameters and learn from data in a online manner. This would be particularly useful in systems that experience rapid changes, such as those caused by scale-out processes or virtual machine migrations. This approach could be explored in conjunction with existing work on adaptive DDoS mitigation systems. This is because it could facilitate the development of systems that learn from data to minimize the frequency and duration of DDoS attacks, thereby improving the effectiveness of DDoS mitigation. This potential application for BoAnon is expected to be a focus of ongoing research. Determining the quality of large RDF datasets remains a challenging task, especially when relying on prior knowledge. Our proposed quality evaluation framework, called DistQualityAssessment, utilizes a distributed approach to effectively handle large datasets by dividing them into manageable parts and evaluating their quality independently. This approach yields two primary benefits: it enhances performance on large datasets and reduces evaluation times. In experiments, we demonstrated that DistQualityAssessment ensures precise quality evaluations and outperforms a centralized approach in terms of scalability. Furthermore, we compared DistQualityAssessment to prominent RDF validation tools, such as ShapeExpress and ValidTime, under varying conditions, revealing that it excels in quality evaluation times while maintaining precision. Additionally, we found that DistQualityAssessment is particularly suited for quality evaluation of large datasets in cloud environments. In these settings, it utilizes the capabilities of distributed cloud computers to achieve even faster evaluation times. The code and data employed in our research are now available for public access, representing a first step towards developing quality evaluation standards for RDF datasets. In this context, we also outline possible directions for enhancing DistQualityAssessment, including the integration of new quality evaluation algorithms and methodologies for assessing data integrity. This framework is compatible with prominent RDF stores, including Apache Jena and AllegroGraph, and supports the evaluation of complex data types, such as literals with HTTP links, combining both effectiveness and efficiency. DistQualityAssessment is compatible with prominent RDF validation languages, including SHAPE and ShACL. In this context, we also compared DistQualityAssessment to AllegroGraph's built-in validation capabilities, revealing that it outperforms them in quality evaluation times. Nevertheless, this framework is in need of further development to address various other challenges in quality evaluation, such as handling cyclic references, evaluating property paths, supporting additional data types, and integrating new quality evaluation algorithms. This study explores the properties of minimum density power divergence (MDP) estimators when applied to various important processes, including independent increment and Markov processes. We examine how MDP estimators contrast with maximum likelihood (ML) estimators in such scenarios. Due to the complexity of calculating ML estimates for several processes, we focus on the MDP estimate as a alternative. We are particularly interested in understanding the behavior of MDP estimates when the sampling size is finite, a scenario that has not been extensively researched in the literature. We are looking to answer questions such as: Under finite sampling sizes, do MDP estimates share the same properties as their ML counterparts? Do MDP estimates and their ML counterparts converge at a similar rate? To address these questions, we investigate the properties of MDP estimates and their relationships with ML estimates. We establish the conditions under which the MDP estimate converges to the desired parameter, the rate of this convergence, and the relationship with the ML estimate, including its rate of convergence. Our findings can be applied to several important processes, including ARMA, AR, MA, and Poisson processes. We also provide the results of simulations that verify our theoretical findings. We observe that, under finite sampling sizes, the MDP estimate converges to the desired parameter at a rate of $O_(2\delta)$, where $\delta$ is the parameter of the power divergence distance, and that this rate of convergence is better than that of the ML estimate when $2\delta$ is less than 1/2. Additionally, we find that the MDP estimate shares the same rate of convergence with the ML estimate when $2\delta$ is greater than or equal to 1/2. We also establish the conditions under which the MDP estimate and its ML counterpart converge to the same distribution. We provide specific values of the parameters that satisfy these conditions for several important processes. We conclude that the MDP estimate is a viable alternative to the ML estimate, especially when the sampling size is finite and the rate of convergence of the MDP estimate is better than that of the ML estimate. We anticipate that our findings will contribute positively to the advancement of statistics and its applications. We suggest potential research directions related to our study. The Frisbee framework addresses this issue by offering a novel approach that combines automated testing with learning algorithms to effectively evaluate the performance of IoT applications. Unlike conventional testing methods that rely on static strategies, Frisbee develops a dynamic model based on theoretical performance standards and conducts continuous, adaptive testing to identify and address areas that need improvement. Frisbee's unique methodology enables it to overcome limitations associated with conventional testing methods, such as their reliance on static strategies, ability to handle complex systems, and provide a performance guarantee. The sophisticated approach employed by the LHCb team allowed for sensitive measurements of rare processes. Current approaches to training autonomous vehicles using simulation focus on generating detailed 3D models of scenes and reinforcing safe driving practices. However, these methods lack the variety of situations needed for comprehensive vehicle training. To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a novel generative model that creates intricate traffic scenarios while ensuring consistency with real world data. Unlike existing approaches, SceneGen doesn't require explicit rules or label information. Instead, it utilizes a hierarchical structure and minimizes target losses to effectively create plausible and dangerous scenarios. By doing so, SceneGen successfully generates diverse and coherent scenes, as evaluated by metrics including completeness, accuracy, and purity, outperforming existing models and meeting the standards of human annotators. Furthermore, SceneGen's capability to graduate from simple to complex scenarios and its safety guarantees through minimum risk targeting enable continuous progress and stable training. Ultimately, SceneGen demonstrates a notable advancement in traffic scenario generation, surpassing the performance of human annotators and significantly contributing to the development of more robust autonomous vehicle training methods. Alongside our code and data, we are launching the Traffic Scenario Benchmark, a groundbreaking benchmark that assesses autonomous vehicle safety by evaluating their performance in complex scenes generated by SceneGen. This benchmark sets a new standard for evaluating scene generation models and provides a platform for comparing different models and techniques. The code, data, and benchmark are available at https://scenegensb.com. We demonstrate that using a Cayley tree structure, the Ising model can be analytically solved on any connected graph at non-zero temperature, with the configuration interpreted through the symmetries associated with the group of Gelfand-Naimark-Segal representations. This results in a precise expression for the partition function, and reveals a direct connection between the structure of the Cayley tree and its isomorphic relationship with the binary hypercube, allowing us to derive an easy-to-compute expression for the partition function for any connected graph. Furthermore, we derive a universal formula for the derivative of the free energy and confirm that the connectivity of the graph is the sole determinant of the critical temperature. Additionally, we establish that the connective structure of the graph is identical to that of the binary hypercube in the low-temperature limit, and that both the critical temperature and the connective structure of the graph can be understood through the lens of Gelfand-Naimark-Segal representations. Lastly, we predict spin wave oscillations in the Ising model on any connected graph below the critical temperature.

This study presents a novel extension to the Flexible Generalized Minimum Residual Method (FGMRES) iteration, dubbed the compressed $\mathcal{H}$-orthogonalization FG MRES (choF MRES). The core idea of the choF MRES involves adapting the projection onto the subspace generated by the previous iteration vectors, which enhances the method's convergence and precision for large non-normal matrix-related systems. To demonstrate the choF MRES's effectiveness, we examine its performance on a range of cases involving square and non-square systems, including an example drawn from the transport equation. Numerical results indicate that the choF MRES iteration outperforms the standard FGMRES method in terms of iteration count and degree of precision achieved. Furthermore, the algorithm requires minimal additional computational cost per iteration. The implementation of the algorithm is compatible with the PETSc library and the FEniCS project, allowing it to leverage the performance benefits of modern Direct Linear Solver packages via the DLS package. By combining the proposed choF MRES iteration with the Flexible Krylov Subspace Method, the study aims to provide a reliable and efficient solution strategy for large-scale numerical discretization problems. We provide evidence that ergodicity across all directions is not a typical feature of systems with multiple parameters. To this end, we present a continuous standard map with two variables for which we prove the existence of odd acip and, under a specific condition, demonstrate that its joint ergodicity is uncommon. Furthermore, our findings yield an infinite number of scenarios solving an unsolved problem posed by Kalhovskis. Additionally, our research implies that the set distinguishing systems with ergodic properties shared across all directions from those with isolated ergodic properties has positive Lebesgue measure along at least one dimension. Alongside, we offer a theoretical model that illustrates the intricacies of ergodicity in systems with multiple parameters. Finally, we propose a continuation of the approach introduced by Kalhovskis to explore ergodicity in higher-dimensional systems.

The vast amounts of dust observed in molecular clouds can be attributed to the destruction of stars through supernovae, particularly pair-instability and core-collapse events. When combined with massive star interactions, these supernovae generate superbubbles, significantly increasing dust levels within these regions. However, previous models have underestimated the dust amount in this process by ignoring dust creation from supernovae interactions and the dispersion of dust grains throughout the cloud under gravity's influence. To address this, a new method is introduced to track the development of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae within molecular clouds, accounting for dust production from supernovae and its dispersion under gravitational forces. Using this approach, dust evolution is monitored across various cloud types, and the findings suggest that pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae contribute significantly to dust levels in these clouds. Furthermore, this model highlights the importance of dust creation from supernovae interactions and the contribution of dust grains dispersed under gravitational forces. By integrating this approach into existing star formation models, a greater understanding can be gained of the relationship between star formation, supernovae, and the vast dust amounts observed in molecular clouds. The introduction of this model also facilitates the exploration of dust evolution across diverse cloud environments and sheds light on the role of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae in shaping the dust cycles of these clouds. With this model, I also examine the fate of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae, including their contributions to dust creation from supernovae and the dispersion of dust grains throughout the cloud. The model further enables the analysis of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae within different cloud settings and provides insights into the cloud's multi-element abundance structure. The introduction of this model marks an advancement in modeling the development of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae within molecular clouds and paves the way for improved predictions of superbubble evolution and the dust cycles of these clouds. The method introduced in this paper can be applied to any star formation model that tracks the life cycles of massive stars. The model is made publicly available to facilitate the exploration of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae within diverse star formation scenarios and to contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between star formation, supernovae, and the vast dust amounts observed in molecular clouds. The model is also compatible with the SEvolution of Stars (SES) model, a comprehensive star formation model that tracks the life cycles of stars within molecular clouds, and can be integrated with the SES model to facilitate the exploration of pair-instability

To address the challenge of 3D object detection in far-field scenarios, this paper leverages a combined approach that incorporates both sensor-agnostic and sensor-specific methods for processing RGB and lidar data. The proposed framework, MultiScale Detector (MSD), utilizes a series of iterative, feature ascending methods to process data from both sources. Unlike traditional two-stage approaches, MSD includes a protocol for combining processed features from both sensors before entering the detection phase. In tests on the waymo open dataset, MSD demonstrates superior performance compared to existing sensor-agnostic and sensor-specific methods, surpassing averages of precision and recall by 2.3% and 6.2% respectively, and achieving a far-field precision of 84.8%. The code for this paper has been made available on the GitHub platform.

A new approach has been proposed by researchers to accelerate the creation of highly energetic molecular states using artificial neural networks. This model, developed in the context of quantum machine learning, learns from previous calculations of the same molecular structure and associated energy levels to predict a large number of complex molecular states. Despite being trained to reproduce only a limited set of existing energy levels, the model demonstrates remarkable effectiveness in preparing a wide range of quantum states on the molecular potential energy surface. In particular, it exceeds the performance of conventional methods in predicting state energies and probabilities for interactions with photons. Tests conducted on the ANI-CCSD(T) data sets for water and ethylene demonstrated the model's ability to accurately model potential energy curves for low-energy states and rotational constants. However, it also struggled to model a higher-energy state and rotational coefficients for water when using the same training data. To validate the model's potential, researchers calculated dynamic processes involving these molecules, such as diffusion, chemical reaction rates, and radiationless transitions, and found that it accurately models energy surfaces even when applied to extended systems. This implies that the model can be an valuable tool for studying complex molecular phenomena. In order to facilitate widespread use, the researchers have made the pre-trained models available for download. In addition, the work highlights the opportunity for further advancements in the field of quantum chemistry through the development of more effective artificial intelligence algorithms. The associated database, which includes previously unreported energy levels for water and ethylene, can be utilized to drive future breakthroughs. The researchers also introduced a novel feature called the "quantum node" that can be employed to model energy surfaces for larger molecules. In this framework, the artificial neural network is trained to model energy surfaces by ranking the importance of different orbital combinations, known as amplitudes, rather than predicting energy levels directly. As a result, the model can be finely tuned to focus on previously unmodeled areas of the energy surface, making it an exciting development for quantum chemistry. In this work, the "quantum node" framework was used to model a new energy level in water and an amide state in ethylene, achieving results on par with the most advanced current methods. The researchers open the door to further innovation by releasing the "quantum node" code publicly, giving other researchers the opportunity to adapt this novel approach for their own applications. In doing so, they provide amplitudes for all molecular states studied in this research as part of the associated database, giving potential users a chance to compare their results directly with the models' outputs.

This study investigates an innovative approach to mapping organs using a non-parametric transformation model, based on a method called kernel regression, which can compensate for noisy data. Initially, we employed a traditional parameteric model along with a spatio-temporal B-spline for mapping a patient, and tested its robustness with noisy data. Subsequently, we developed a new approach using kernel regression, which was validated by comparing it to the temporal B-spline model in both simulated and real-world scenarios. The results showed that kernel regression offers greater resistance to noisy data. A further analysis indicated that kernel regression maintains accurate mapping across multiple surgeries, with a method for adjusting its hyperparameters through a metric that evaluates the effects of noisy data. Ultimately, our research demonstrated that kernel regression yields reliable mappings across varied surgical environments, making it an attractive alternative to conventional modeling techniques. However, further studies are required to explore its applications in different surgical contexts. This study provides valuable contributions to the development of organ modeling systems, which are essential for enhancing surgical planning and execution. Additionally, we present our approach as a suite of algorithms and code, available for public use and adaptation in different surgical scenarios. While self-supervised flow estimation has achieved significant progress, there remains a persistent issue: occlusions. Our research aims to address this challenge by developing a method to estimate flows without the need for correspondences. We propose a self-supervised approach, where a neural network predicts both correspondence and occlusion probabilities in an alternative representation of pixel values. This prediction enables us to formulate a discriminative loss function for flow estimation, which can be executed without requiring correspondence. We evaluate our approach through comparisons with existing self-supervised and supervised methods on the KITTI dataset, which reveals improved performance when there are occlusions. Furthermore, our approach proves comparable to state-of-the-art self-supervised methods in non-occluded scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/zyang12 SelfSupFlow.

Deep learning techniques have significantly raised performance levels for various classification tasks, but most of these methods are power-hungry and difficult to integrate into mobile devices and embedded systems due to their substantial memory requirements. To address this challenge, we present a novel, compact neural network model called the Hyperplane Expert Network (HEN) that has a compact design, minimal weight pruning, and utilizes an efficient sign-based learning algorithm.HEN's performance is comparable to that of Advanced Neural Networks (ANNs) in multiple classification tasks while achieving a 15-20 times reduction in memory consumption and 2-4 times decrease in computational resources compared to annealed neural networks. Furthermore, Hen's performance is on par with ANNs in multiple classification tasks and demonstrates its superiority over various deep learning expert networks variants across multiple benchmark datasets. Additionally, Hen successfully competes with ANNs in multi-task classification scenarios, showcasing its capacity to handle complex, real-world data. The Hen model's efficiency is achieved through a unique combination of weight pruning and compact design, along with the sign-based learning algorithm, which allows it to operate with significantly reduced memory and computational resources. This innovative approach not only makes Hen an attractive option for embedded systems but also paves the way for further exploration of efficient deep learning models. This study introduces an innovative technique for determining the function and analyzing the characteristics of sundials using photos taken by citizens and combines this with historical research on sundials in Indonesia. As sundials are present in strategic locations with notable views, they have the potential to be effective landmarks for community engagement and education about science and culture. In this research, we explore the characteristics of sundials in Indonesia by examining their mathematics and cultural aspects, as well as their historical development. The effectiveness of electron probes in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs) can be significantly enhanced through the use of electrostatic phase plates (EPPs). EPPs modify the electron probe cross-section using a thin coating with a periodic design, affecting the probe size and current density due to their interaction with the electron beam. This study investigates how various design features of EPPs, including fill-factor and pixel pattern, influence electron probes, with a focus on post-column EPP applications. By simulating the interaction between electrons and different design parameters, we investigated the relationship between probe size, current density, and EPP orientation. Our findings reveal that rotating the EPP by 45 degrees can reduce large diameter components, thereby reducing the average diameter, and that filling-factor and pixel-pattern effects are more pronounced at low probe voltages. This research provides theoretical foundations for optimal EPP design, and includes a discussion on the limitations of current simulation methods and potential improvements. Furthermore, we present experimental results showing significant improvements in probe performance, with reduced diameters and increased current densities, achieved using an optimal EPP design in a post-column TEM application. This has resulted in improved signal-to-noise ratio in analog image recording, and potentially has implications for image charging in TEM. The results are applied to evaluate the renormalized interaction effects on the quasiparticle density of states and the renormalized specific heat in doped graphene. A notable deviation from the universal behavior is found for the quasiparticle velocity at low doping levels. Additionally, the renormalized interaction strength at low doping levels is found to be in poor agreement with existing models, showing a disparity of approximately 30%. This discrepancy is attributed to an inappropriate application of the non-interacting density-functional theory to calculate the density of states in those models. The goal of the MaskedSpeech system is to enhance the naturalness and emotional impact of text-to-speech synthesis.  This involves generating multiple simultaneous sentences, but only keeping a few words from each sentence, in an attempt to replicate the complex and dynamic conversations found in everyday life.  Instead of generating entire sentences, the system uses a different approach, in which each word is represented as a function of all the other words being spoken at the same time, with a specific focus on speech that has been masked.  This approach involves the use of a single, unified probability distribution to model all of the words being spoken at the same time, and producing the final TTS synthesis through a process of iterative refinement.  When tested using a large dataset of conversational text, the MaskedSpeech system was found to produce a significant improvement in naturalness and emotional impact, and the system's performance can be further enhanced through the use of additional training on a dataset of dramatic reading.  Experimental results indicate that the proposed system offers a more effective way of producing TTS synthesis, one that is capable of successfully mimicking the complex interactions found in conversations.  The proposed system is also shown to offer several major advantages over traditional TTS methods, in which the producer of the synthesis is the sole authority, and the potential for a more realistic and engaging listening experience is also explored. We examine the presence of stable orbital waves in a one-dimensional, variable-velocity Bose-Einstein condensate model, featuring an anharmonic oscillator, by applying existing methods for both linear and nonlinear stability analyses. Our analysis of the anharmonic oscillator reveals that its effects can be accounted for by modifying the linear part of the equation, resulting in a modified Klein-Gordon equation. However, the modification causes a shift in the value of nonlinear ground state energy from $-|\mu|^2$ to $-\mu \mu^*$. Interestingly, this changed dynamics enables orbital stability of the anharmonic oscillator within the anisotropic region, despite the loss of stability of the harmonic oscillator. Notably, the anharmonic oscillator's influence can be understood as a linear stabilization mechanism, which in turn facilitates the superfluidity of atoms moving in a potential with an harmonic structure. This is confirmed by both numerical simulations and analytical arguments. Additionally, we observe that the anharmonic oscillator's effects can be viewed as adding an effective potential that shifts the symmetry breaking point. This behavior is further illustrated by a simple normal form analysis, which reveals that the anharmonic oscillator can be effectively represented by a family of linearly perturbed structures. Finally, we find that the anharmonic oscillator can be used to control the orbital stability of the condensate by switching its stability via the anharmonic potential, despite being located at an anisotropic distance. This is shown to result in a modulated frequency spectrum, which responds differently to changes in the anharmonic potential's amplitude and number of components. This study provides new insights into the dynamics of Bose-Einstein condensates in one-dimensional systems, revealing the impact of anharmonic oscillators on orbital waves and offering a potential tool for controlling the condensate's stability. This work is a initial step towards a more comprehensive understanding of anharmonic oscillators in one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate systems, which can be extended to higher dimensional systems through the application of established variable coefficient techniques. This knowledge gap affects our understanding of scalar field theories that possess multiple
global symmetries, which can be relevant in models that incorporate extra dimensions.
In this research, we examine the properties of Q-balls while assuming that one of these
symmetries is held constant.
Our analysis indicates that when the two symmetries have comparable charges, there is a
four-dimensional solution space describing Q-ball equilibrium states.
In contrast, there is only a two-dimensional solution space when one symmetry has a much
stronger influence than the other.
Additionally, we found that the stabilizing symmetries play a significant role in the
conservation of charge, with the total conserved charge equating to the sum of the
individual charges for each symmetry, during both steady-state and non-steady-state
conditions.
Our research also reveals that in theories where the potential energy of the scalar
field is flat between its vacuum points, Q-balls with zero-size can actually form, and
we demonstrate this by solving a set of complex nonlinear equations.

wave observations, particularly in scenarios involving the merger of two Q-ball objects.

We investigate the relationship between an abstract L-function associated with a graph and its topological covering surfaces. By defining L-functions for graphs, we can establish connections between their spectral characteristics and the spectral characteristics of the L-functions. These connections are tested on specific examples, including a particular graph whose abstract L-functions correspond to the L-functions of the surfaces that are covering of the graph. The results indicate that the abstract L-functions can provide valuable information about the surfaces that are covering of the graph, and vice versa. Moreover, there are implications for conjectures related to the distribution of zeros of L-functions, especially the Hilbert-Polya conjecture. By examining the relationship between the abstrac L-functions and their corresponding covering surfaces, we can bypass the limitations of current methods for constructing examples of L-functions with specific zero locations. In particular, we can construct examples of L-functions with maximal analytic continuation across a plane boundary, and thus, potentially influencing the behavior of the Riemann zeta function at s=1.1. Additionally, our findings introduce a new framework for studying the properties of L-functions through the characteristics of the graphs from which they originate. This approach also enables the classification of L-functions based on the topological properties of their associated graphs and covering surfaces. As a result, the abstract L-functions provide a fresh perspective on understanding the complex relationships between graph theory, topology, and number theory. This research proposes a framework for identifying neutral long-lived particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and future colliders. Depending on the decay length of these particles, various production processes and decay channels can be examined. When the decay length is short, focusing on hadronic decay modes with missing energy is optimal. For longer decay lengths, decays into leptons or photons become more significant. The optimal search strategy greatly depends on the magnitude of the decay length. For instance, at the LHC with 14 TeV proton beams and 100 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, our model indicates that a decay length of less than 0.6 mm is required for hadronic searches, 0.8 mm for leptonic searches, and 0.4 mm for photonic searches. An extension of previous work, this framework also considers several key factors, including beamstrahlung effects, TTbar background, and the impact of additional long-lived neutral particles on background and signal. Additionally, this framework is applicable to various types of colliders and can be adapted to different search tools and experiments. By integrating the DDILLP tool, this framework provides a comprehensive package that includes Monte Carlo simulations for long-lived neutral particles and is available for collaboration with experimental teams. Consequently, a 5 sigma discovery limit for the production cross-section of a specific long-lived neutral particle can be determined for various decay lengths and production and decay modes. However, the effect of contextual variance itself is often overlooked, which can lead to misleading conclusions about these shifts. This paper highlights the importance of considering variance in context, demonstrating through experiments that changes in contextual variance significantly impact the interpretation of semantic shifts. Additionally, it proposes a more comprehensive framework for analyzing language models that takes into account the role of variance in context. The extensive use of emails by research institutions makes them vulnerable to security breaches if their email systems are not adequately maintained, which could have serious consequences, including data theft. As these institutions also frequently collaborate, their cooperation can be compromised due to concerns about security. To address this issue, a secure collaboration framework has been developed, which builds on existing technologies while ensuring user anonymity and secures email communications and data transfers. This framework consists of several components, including a login feature, user registration, collaboration setup, secure email delivery, file transfer, and anonymity maintenance. We evaluate the performance of this framework through a set of operations, including sending emails, creating collaborations, transferring files, and maintaining anonymity, which are conducted simultaneously by a large number of users. The assessment is carried out on a cloud platform that combines computing power from multiple providers. The outcome shows that the performance of this secure email system is comparable to that of regular email systems, despite providing enhanced security features. This suggests that even the most resource-intensive applications can be executed safely within this framework. Furthermore, an investigation into the cryptographic techniques employed here reveals that existing protocols may suffer from inefficiencies, allowing for further improvements. As a result, this secure email system can serve as a foundation for other collaboration scenarios. Ultimately, this framework is capable of ensuring the anonymity of users and securing email communications and data transfers, thus making it an effective tool for safe cooperation. This research is accompanied by source code and technical details to facilitate enhancement and modification. As such, it is made available under suitable open-source licenses. In cuprates, we propose that an exceptional van Hove singularity, arising from a Lifshitz transition associated with a nodal anti-node merger at the Fermi level, drives the underlying physics of the superconducting phase. This idea is supported by a combination of insights from theoretical and experimental sources. The life cycle of this singularity, influenced by electron correlations, forms the basis of our proposed framework. As a result, the associated peak in the spectral function contributes significantly to various experimental characteristics, including the onset of superconductivity, anomalous transport properties, and the structural changes observed in cuprates. Furthermore, our model incorporates a competition between two life cycle stages of this singularity, where the driven movement of anti-nodes precedes a return to nodal character across the transition. This competition gives rise to diverse phenomena depending on the electron masses of end members, leading to the diversity of cuprate behaviors. Our framework is realized in the context of the (1111) cuprate Ba$_2$CuO$_4$ using accurate band structure and is validated through the analysis of peak-related physics across multiple phases of this material. By offering a unifying theoretical explanation for the underlying physics of the superconducting phase, our model provides a new perspective on the complexity of cuprate behaviors. Ultimately, we propose that the exceptional van Hove singularity, driven by a Lifshitz transition associated with a nodal anti-node merger at the Fermi level, may be the primary factor responsible for the diversity of cuprate behaviors. Although Gd enhances efficiency, it also complicates neutron-energy spectrum analysis by introducing a prominent gamma background. A novel deconvolution technique for simultaneous gamma-ray analysis is now available, enabling researchers to reconstruct neutron energy spectra despite substantial gamma backgrounds. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, researchers analyzed a variety of scenarios, including a simple case with a strong neutron signal and significant gamma contamination at the 5-15 MeV energy range, a complex case with multiple gamma lines to accounting for neutron decay and scattering, and an extreme case with a thin scintillator and extensive gamma absorption. The results showed that the new deconvolution method can accurately recover neutron energy spectra in all scenarios, outperforming traditional analysis methods. Furthermore, researchers found that the new approach can model gamma spectra accurately, providing a comprehensive understanding of the gamma spectrum and allowing for independent analysis of gamma and neutron components. This new technique is expected to significantly enhance the NEUNDIX detector's capability to study neutron decay and facilitate groundbreaking research in neutron physics. The development of this approach can also be applied to other neutron detectors that interact with gamma radiation. The new deconvolution method has been incorporated into the NEUNDIX software package and is available for public use. The code can be obtained from the author upon request. New observations from NASA's TESS and Spitzer by 2020 allow us to examine how star systems' properties influence the diversity of planetary configurations. By analyzing 2020 data, the TESS Exoplanat Catalog consists of 2000 confirmed planets across 4000 candidates, providing us with an ideal dataset to explore this question. However, simply inspecting the distribution of planetary configurations is insufficient, as many of these star systems contain multiple planets, leading to complex configurations. In response, we introduce a method to rank the simplicity or disorder of these systems based on a principle known as Kolmogorov complexity. By applying this approach, we can better understand the diversity of planetary architectures among the newly discovered systems and compare it with the distribution of stellar masses and types. Moreover, we can identify specific configurations that exhibit unique characteristics, such as stability or instability, and determine how often they occur. By utilizing this approach, we can also identify systems that may harbor specific patterns of planetary organization, such as habitable planets or systems with planets in the HZ. Finally, we can rank the list of candidate targets for future missions aimed at identifying biosignatures on planets, such as the PACE mission set to launch in 2029. By utilizing this approach, we can move beyond individual, isolated discoveries and gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between planets within their star systems. Ultimately, this research empowers us to pinpoint the most promising candidates for further analysis and is essential for developing predictive theories about the composition and organization of planetary systems. This research will be continued with enhanced datasets expected from TESS and GAIA in 2023 and 2024, respectively. This work is part of the TESS-UCLA Legacy Science Program, focused on studying the 300 brightest parallax targets from GAIA with TESS, and is expected to result in over 1000 new exoplanet discoveries, providing us with an ideal dataset to explore the architecture of planetary systems. This research is anticipated to yield significant insights into how the formation of planetary systems is influenced by their parent star systems and will offer a comprehensive overview of the field in 2024. The decline of traditional face-to-face community engagement prompts interest in online communities centered on politics. Online users regularly participate in forums, social media, and special interest groups, navigating complex networks that can facilitate the spread of political information and influence voting behaviors. To gain insights into the evolution of online political communities, we develop a theoretical framework that incorporates both collective behavior principles and network dynamics. We then apply this framework to analyze data from a political discussion forum with features of a community, where users post opinions on various topics. Our analysis of community evolution is conducted through the examination of user posting history, focusing on the interplay between users' interests, the attraction to existing communities, and community dynamics that emerge from individual interactions. Our results showcase the development of community hierarchies, where communities that attract more posts tend to develop over time and serve as parent communities for other communities. Furthermore, our analysis of network dynamics reveals patterns that contribute to community growth, including the formation of connections between users who share similar interests, the rotation of community membership, and the attachment of new users to existing communities. Our findings are complemented by visualizations that display community evolution and reveal correlations with prominent global politics events. Ultimately, our study provides a theoretical framework and concrete examples that demonstrate the complex evolution of online political communities through individual interactions, emphasizing the significance of community dynamics that emerge from shared opinions and attraction to existing communities. Along with implications for the spread of political information and influence, our research paves the way for the development of algorithms that anticipate online community growth and development. Lastly, our work highlights potential applications for improving community engagement and user experience within online platforms. We conclude by discussing potential directions for further research, including the extension of our framework to additional online communities and the integration of offline data to enhance understanding of online community evolution. Along with, we explore the possibility of utilizing our framework to develop predictive models for forecasting online community growth and development. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for the development of theoretical and computational approaches that aim to tackle the complex evolution of online communities through individual interactions. Along with, we hope to contribute to the advancement of research at the intersection of online communities, big data analytics, and computational social science. Lastly, we look forward to sharing our work with researchers across multiple disciplines. Determining whether a set of rational functions in one variable is continuous can be challenging, as it involves evaluating limits that may extend to infinity. However, we demonstrate that this task can be accomplished efficiently by utilizing a polynomial-time computable decision method, based on evaluating the rational functions at an infinitely large point that is easily computable. This method allows us to prove decision problems related to algebraic dynamical systems to be solvable in NP, even when these systems are defined by irrational mappings. Furthermore, our method enables us to solve other problems related to the evaluation of algebraic dynamical systems at infinite points, and can decisionally determine whether a given rational function is equivalent to a system of algebraic dynamical systems, by means of an infinite-point evaluation that is computationally efficient. Additionally, we explore connections to other decision problems in NP, and discuss possible applications of our method to systems defined over fields other than the complex numbers. Lastly, we note that our method yields an infinitely large point that is easily computable, but determining the computable values at finite points requires a significantly more complex computation. This is accompanied by an analysis of the implications of our method to system dynamics, and we discuss possible future directions in this area. We demonstrate that using a local-functional representation of signals, particularly those in low dimensions, can significantly enhance their representational versatility, even across different tasks, by reducing the impact of intrinsic variability. This approach to signal analysis offers a self-consistent framework for combining multiple signal features, addressing concerns about data quality, and providing a meaningful way to measure signal quality. The method is tested in a classification scenario using both artificial and real-world datasets, which shows that it can create robust models capable of generalizing well, even when presented with new types of low-dimensional signals that were not part of the training data. This leads to the opportunity to explore new perspectives on the fundamental concepts of probability theory and the generalization of signals in higher dimensions. Human observations suggest that living beings fall into a continuous spectrum of animacy, ranging from simple components to complex, self-sustaining entities. Our concept of visual categorizability addresses the spectrum's initial portion, covering basic features to moderate combinations, while agency represents the later section, encompassing self-directed objects to complex, autonomous living beings. To explore the animacy spectrum, we develop a neural network that learns to classify objects as animated or not, based on either visual categorizability or agency, or both, using multiple linear regressors. By combining both factors, the network significantly improves its predictions. Additionally, we find that visual categorizability and agency exhibit distinct patterns in a feature space, and that certain neural network features that code for agency are delayed in development. These delays suggest that simple models of learning through association may not adequately capture the development of animated entity recognition. Human studies confirm that young children distinguish basic components from complex objects, and that the concept of agency emerges later in childhood. Our findings provide computational and empirical evidence for the animacy spectrum, and suggest that visual categorizability and agency are fundamental dimensions governing this spectrum. We have developed QHoare, a quantum relational Hoare logic that enables program validators to accurately assess the relationship between programs' input-output pairs. By leveraging quantum relational Hoare logic, programmers can ensure the correctness of quantum programs by validating the behavior of programs in relation to specific input-output pairs. Furthermore, QHoare allows pre and postconditions to be specified for quantum programs, making it possible to validate the correctness of programs in relation to certain conditions. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of QHoare through a quantum program written in Q# and validated its correctness using the F# interpreter for Hoare logic. Additionally, we have shown that QHoare is capable of handling multiple relational predicates and can handle the quantum entanglement phenomenon known as quantum teleportation. All of our examples are available online at the QHoare GitHub repository. The GitHub repository contains the quantum program, its validator, the relational predicate, the F# interpreter for Hoare logic, and the example tests. We're examining this phenomenon within a closed environment, such as a gathering, using a model that incorporates a power-law distribution to represent the varying levels of infection risk among individuals. In our model, a super-spreader is someone who infects a number of people greater than one, with the specific number varying according to the distribution. We're comparing our model's results to standard epidemiological models, specifically the SIR and SEIR models, by incorporating it into a gravitational simulation.
