A Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Model (HiP-RSSM) is a dynamic system model that consists of a variable-based state space model and a neural network-based parameter model. This type of model has recently achieved significant success in learning and inference for complex systems and time series data. However, HiP-RSSM education lacks a comprehensive theoretical foundation, particularly when the state and hidden parameters follow non-linear trajectories. In this study, we introduce an innovative algorithm for HiP-RSSM education based on an expected maximization approach, and we derive a precise expression for the educational loss decrease. Moreover, we prove the convergence of this algorithm under mild conditions. We also evaluate the algorithm with multiple HiP-RSSM architectures, including state and hidden dynamic systems that are linear, non-linear, and mixed, and we demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency on various education scenarios, including fixed and moving hidden parameters, as well as state and hidden trajectories that are independent and correlated. Our results show the algorithm's effectiveness and versatility. We expect this study to contribute to the development of theoretical education frameworks for HiP-RSSM. All source code is openly available at https://github.com/hjdwang/HiP-RSSM-education.

Consider three independent random matrices from the COE, CSE, and CES ensembles respectively. If the first two matrices share the same eigenvalue distribution under the sole condition that their respective eigenvalues and corresponding singular value spectra are equal, then the compatibility condition implies that the third matrix must conditionaly share the same eigenvalue distribution with the first two. This result is shown to hold not just in the large N limit, but also for finite N through a combination of analytical and numerical methods. The analysis of the associated joint probability measures reveals a rotation in angle that occurs in the conditionally free case, resulting in a branching in probability measures under the free and conditional free settings. Further analysis of the rotated measures yields insights into their scaling limits, consisting of the product of a deterministic function and a differential of a Brownian motion, and reveals a distinct branch point at $\sqrt{4-\pi^2}$ for the scaling limits of the COE, CSE, and CES ensembles. Additionally, numerical methods are used to compare the sizes of $\frac{\lambda_{max}-\lambda_{min}}{N^{-1/3}}$ for finite N across these three ensembles, showing a hierarchy of COE $\geq$ CSE $\geq$ CES. The branch point is verified through a combination of analytical and numerical methods, and the comparison of edge statistics is carried out through numerical simulation. A related open question remains as to whether the COE and CSE ensembles share the same large N eigenvalue distribution. If so, it would imply that the condition of equal spectra and corresponding singular value spectra are sufficient for freeness to imply equality of eigenvalue distributions. A positive answer to this question would have far-reaching consequences for the study of unitary invariant matrices and their relationships with free limits. We present a new construction for a genus 2 curve, C, in terms of another genus 1 curve, D, and a non-hyperelliptic genus 3 curve, E. The relationship between these curves is defined by specific coverings: E covers C, which in turn covers D. This construction contradicts prior beliefs that no genus 2 curve could be made up of three genus 3 curves as proposed by Hartshorne in his paper 'Ample subvarieties of compact manifolds of small codimension'. Our proof draws from ideas presented in a problem set by Beauville and also incorporates some concepts used by Ellingsgaard in 'Counter-Example to Hartshorne's Conjecture'. The strategy involves creating a specific object, constructing an intermediate step, and then showing that this intermediate step has properties desired for our new genus 2 curve, C. Finally, we demonstrate that certain values of parameters can lead to a counter-example of Hartshorne's Conjecture, which may have interest on their own.  Although our method fails to give the most sought-after examples, it still presents novel ways to build genus 2 curves through multiple genus 3 curves and may be used to create other interesting situations.  To further this research, the questions and potential directions for investigation presented in the final section could be considered.  In particular, it seems there may be additional cases where our construction yields counter-examples to Hartshorne's Conjecture, especially when the genus 3 curve, E, is a double cover of a genus 2 curve, F, which in turn is a double cover of D.  Additionally, when E and F are hyperelliptic, it is possible to construct a genus 2 curve, C, as the quotient of a genus 4 curve, but it is unknown if this construction is valid when E and F are not hyperelliptic.  Therefore, further investigation is required to determine the full scope of this construction and its potential applications to Hartshorne's Conjecture.  Moreover, it is also unknown if this construction may be utilized for other conjectures, such as the Bogomolov Minimal Autonomy for surfaces.  Thus, exploring this construction for other situations could lead to additional counter-examples to these conjectures.  Finally, when the genus 3 curve, E, is not hyperelliptic, it is possible to construct a non-trivial automorphism of a certain surface, which may have interest in its own right

This study conducts a comprehensive review of methods employed to examine polarization in social networks through the study of individual actors. It evaluates and scrutinizes four methods used to determine the polarization of individuals in social networks. These methods include utilizing local community structure, analyzing relationship types, considering degree distribution, and examining the composition of community structure. The study also provides examples of polarization measurement methods used in science through the re-examination of existing studies. It proposes an enhanced approach for measuring polarization, focusing on individual actors within a social network, and offers technical details for implementing this approach. We examine the stability of states in multilayer networks with non-negative weights by introducing a simplified method that leverages node degrees. This approach allows us to classify the stability of states in single-layer networks and identify unstable states in multilayer networks. Furthermore, we apply the smallest eigenvalue of a Jacobian matrix to validate our method and provide a measure of stability for multilayer networks. Additionally, we utilize synthetic and real-world data to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our method enables the analysis of stability in multilayer networks through the calculation of a critical cutting angle, which can be adjusted to identify unstable states and monitor the dissemination of information or disease spread within complex networks. However, our approach also offers a more efficient alternative to existing methods, such as pair approximation, especially for large networks. We illustrate the advantages of our method by comparing it to pair approximation in two examples. We also utilize our method to investigate the impact of different weight ranges on the spread of information or disease in multilayer networks. Our method provides a new perspective on the study of complex networks, allowing us to distinguish between stable and unstable states, monitor the dissemination process, and compare our results with established methods. Roudeault recently defined operators that map differential modules to derived differential modules, establishing a connection between differential modules and Boger-Witt integrals. In this research, we extend this concept by proving that these operators share common properties when restricted to linear differential modules and certain subgroups of Galois groups, ultimately leading to the discovery of a relationship with local zeta functions. This relationship is then utilized to derive bounds for the lengths of periods in the context of Abelian varieties. Additionally, we establish that certain operators can be represented as a combination of another operator, namely the operation of twisting, under specific conditions related to Galois groups. This research also covers the case of abelian varieties and Jason Bell's work on hyperresolutions. Consequently, this results in new estimates for the lengths of periods, both generally and for specific instances, including abelian varieties and multiple Sheaf theory. This new approach to understanding periods emerges from this framework, emphasizing its potential to provide a more unified understanding of this concept. Furthermore, this research paves the way for exploring the connection between differential modules, local zeta functions, and periods in the broader context of mixed differential modules and their connections to motivic Galois groups. Ultimately, this could ultimately provide new insights into the fundamental problem of Baertschiger and Deligault regarding the volumes of period spaces. This research is complemented by a newly introduced software tool that demonstrates the applied aspects of our findings through interactive visualizations. This includes a graphical representation of the bound of period lengths for certain Abelian varieties and its relation to local zeta functions, demonstrating the practical utility of this theoretical research. This software is designed to be easily customizable and is made available under the terms of the Apache License 2.0, with its source code freely accessible on GitHub. Faults introduced during programming can be identified through a testing environment with an automated algorithm that simulates how experienced programmers work. The algorithm in question uses a method called generalization, where it identifies specific instances of errors and their underlying causes, then uses this understanding to improve its own performance. Despite being effective, the algorithm's underlying principles and its effectiveness in various scenarios remain unexplored. To gain insight into its real-world applicability, we developed a simple automated testing tool using Python and subjected it to a series of tests in both a controlled lab environment and with real users. The results show that the algorithm can learn from its mistakes and become even more efficient at finding errors with each new type of fault it encounters. However, its ability to generalize across similar errors is limited, and it performs best in scenarios that resemble its training data. Additionally, we found that the algorithm's ability to correct errors is comparable to its ability to find them, and it can learn to correct errors more effectively with each new correction attempt. Finally, we observed that the algorithm's performance can vary significantly depending on how the programming task is structured, and it is most effective when the faults in question have a clear underlying cause and can be corrected through a simple modification of the associated variables. Overall, our study provides valuable data that can be used to develop more sophisticated automated testing algorithms, and it shows that the basic principles of the generalization algorithm are effective in a wide range of scenarios. The data collected and the insights gained into the algorithm's performance also present opportunities for further theoretical research into the properties and behavior of complex systems that can learn from their mistakes. The outcomes of this study are also being applied to improve the performance of another system responsible for identifying errors in scientific proofs. Late attention-based models like BERT have dominated the NLP scene, yet the need remains for a task-agnostic model that can efficiently leverage multiple tasks with minimal data. In response, HyperPrompt proposes a novel approach centered on HyperNetworks. By establishing a method to automatically learn task-specific prompt embeddings for BERT, HyperPrompt demonstrates significant gains in model efficiency and enhanced performance on multiple tasks. In particular, it showcases how using HyperNetworks leads to the creation of a compact model that achieves 147 tasks on the GLUE dataset with just 1.9 million parameters. Moreover, HyperPrompt achieves notable improvements in semantic role labeling, named entity recognition, and sentence classification, achieving a score of 93.5 on the SOTS dataset and outperforming state-of-the-art low-parameter models on the CoQA dataset. The code and data for HyperPrompt are now available at https://github.com/ghrua/HyperPrompt. We develop a straightforward, distributed algorithm that enables a node to accurately calculate the size of a connected network of identical nodes within one iteration in networks modeled as undirected graphs. The algorithm is designed for networks that are fully connected and feature non-adaptive changes in node weights. It requires each node to randomly generate a unique, relatively prime number for a multi-node system. In networks modeled as directed graphs, the algorithm fails to provide reliable size estimates. To address this limitation, we introduce an adapted version of the algorithm, capable of estimating the size of directed networks through a recursive approach, although it requires prior knowledge of specific graph characteristics. Simulations demonstrate the efficiency and speed of the algorithm in various settings. Furthermore, we analyze its complexity in relation to node weight dynamics and distribution. The algorithm has practical applications, such as helping nodes estimate their place in the order of updated weights and effectively adapting to changing network conditions. We examine the performance of queue length prediction methods in high-speed network environments. Our assessment indicates that Phytion and Wang's 2008 nonparametric method surpasses in accuracy traditional parametric approaches, especially in scenarios with bursty traffic and limited observation windows. Our research expands upon Phytion and Wang's work by utilizing a broader range of service times and network loads. Our key contribution includes a new fast queue length detection method, leveraging Phytion and Wang's nonparametric technique, which detects queue lengths in $O(1)$ time and potentially applies to broader context schemes. We integrate this method into an enhanced general purpose network protocol, demonstrating its effectiveness through simulations in artificial and real-world environments. Our results show that the protocol's performance is comparable to traditional algorithms while providing the beneficial aspect of low queue length errors. We further incorporate this protocol as a module for an autonomous vehicle network system, showcasing its success in preventing queue storms and reducing wait times at intersections. We also propose the concept of bursty traffic detection and corresponding queue planning through collaborative effort between network nodes. Furthermore, we present a theoretical approach to optimizing queue sizes, but acknowledge the challenge of implementing this efficiently in high-speed network environments. Despite this, we argue that our work paves the way for future research and development of optimized queue schemes in high-speed network systems. We are also seeking to collaborate with experts in this field through our proposed ideas. We have already successfully applied our queue length detection method in the context of fusion networks, as shown by the low queue length errors achieved in those systems. This paper examines beam loss incidence in circular particle accelerators. It is common for beam to be diverted or lost due to various mechanisms such as design flaws, user-generated sources, natural phenomena, and technical malfunctions at critical beam shutdown ports. Understanding beam loss etiology is crucial for designing safety-oriented shutdown systems and ensuring personnel protection at critical areas. This paper outlines a diversity-intensive approach that is part of an international effort to gather diverse perspectives on beam loss experiences across various circular accelerators. It highlights notable cases of significant beam loss observed at various facilities, such as the Large Hadron Collider, the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider, the Keck-Peterborough Experimental Facility, the Linac, the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, and the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator, and emphasizes the importance of open communication and data sharing to address beam loss-related safety concerns. Ultimately, exchanging best practices and successful strategies for managing beam loss could significantly benefit the global accelerator community. It is also proposed to present case studies and host discussions on critical beam loss incidents at future Advanced Particle Accelerator Community Workshops. It is hoped that this approach will facilitate learning from experienced accelerator operators and help identify best practices for managing beam loss. It is also intended to encourage open communication about beam loss experiences and facilitate the development of safety-oriented shutdown systems to protect personnel at critical beam shutdown ports. Established in 1899 by David Jacobus Pyper, the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory in Groningen served as the primary institution for conducting the Duke of Albany's Planetary Survey. However, due to local politics and a less favorable location, the laboratory struggled to secure funding and support. In contrast, the Planetary Survey's secondary site in Leiden flourished and became the more prominent institution. This study analyzes various aspects of the two institutions' activities, personnel, and contributions to astronomy from 1900 to 1940, comparing their performance and outcomes. A statistical evaluation of the institutions' work revealed the Kapteyn Laboratory in Groningen to be substantially less efficient in achieving results, despite both institutions producing notable contributions to astronomy. Factors such as the laboratories' research focus, staff composition, and publication rates are examined to explain the observed differences. The study suggests that, to some extent, the institutions' effectiveness could be attributed to the staff appointments, implying that employees' previous research experiences significantly influenced the results obtained. The analysis also raises questions about the relationships between research focus, staff composition, and outcomes, and suggests that the institutions' effectiveness could be modeled using more in-depth statistical methods. The comparison of the two institutions' activities during the Copernican Year (1937) and the International Astronomical Union's adopted year for celebrating the 400th anniversary of Copernicus' birth, provided an opportunity to evaluate the impact of a major astronomical event on the institutions' research efficiency. The study found significant variations in results produced by the institutions under these special conditions, offering insights into how large-scale events influence astronomical research. The comparison of the two institutions' legacy and impact on astronomy after 1940 showed the Kapteyn Laboratory in Groningen to be less influential in promoting its research and legacy compared to the institution in Leiden. The study's findings can inform strategies for promoting the legacies of scientific research institutions, especially in the context of developing countries. The comparison of the two institutions' relationships with their funding bodies, the Dutch government, revealed the institution in Leiden to be more effective in securing funding due to its location in Leiden, a more prominent center of astronomy at the time. The study suggests that the institutions' effectiveness in securing funding could be modeled using more in-depth statistical methods, taking into account various factors such as the institutions' research focus, staff composition, and publication rates. The analysis of the two institutions' interactions with their funding bodies raised questions about the relationships between these factors and funding outcomes.

We also discuss the interconnected aspects of local critic training, norm regularization, and error gradient noise. Ultimately, our framework offers a unifying perspective on the mechanics of local critic training and provides a foundation for in-depth analyses of other neural network architectures. In addition, PATROLA will have the capability to detect dark photons of 0.1-0.9 GeV in energy and transition magnetic monopoles with magnetic charges of 5.5 x 10^-8 to 5.5 x 10^-6 times the fundamental unit of magnetic charge. Furthermore, by observing the scattering of muons off nuclei at low momentum transfers, PATROLA can provide constraints on the existence of light scalar particles in the range of 5 x 10^-3 to 1.2 x 10^-1 eV. The project's sensitivity to these new physics scenarios is the result of a cutting-edge approach that utilizes an integrated fast-slow technique to control systematic errors. Dynamic graph classification a challenging task is where the structure of a graph continuously evolves over time, forbidding the use of a single fixed model. Unlike static graphs, dynamic graphs' changes can be predicted by monitoring the modification history, yet this historical data is often limited to only recent updates. Existing approaches typically combine historical data from the entire evolution history of a graph for classification, ignoring the fact that older updates may have less influence on the current state. In response to these limitations, we introduce the DECENNT model, which utilizes a neural network to map the current graph structure to its corresponding dynamic graph class and utilizes meta-learning to leverage the experience gained from classifying different dynamic graphs. The model is tested on two public datasets, where it demonstrates the capacity to effectively employ very recent updates and leverage more ancient updates, also proving more effective than standard graph neural network baselines. The DECENNT model also excels in prediction tasks on unseen updates, showcasing its value in monitoring dynamic graphs. In addition, an in-depth analysis of the model's performance with various update frequencies and ages provides meaningful insights into its functioning. We tackle the challenge of converging rate analysis for the Neumann network by incorporating the inception depth into the algorithm, resulting in the Nested Neumann algorithm. By assuming the Neumann operator's convergence in L2 norm to L1 norm, we prove the convergence rate of $\frac{1}{\text{inception depth}}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this depth can be viewed as an optimal regularization parameter. Specifically, we show that the Neumann network achieves the largest possible convergence rate of 1 when the inception depth is infinite. Additionally, we derive a relationship between the inception depth and the network's Lipschitz constant, establishing that the convergence rate is inversely proportional to the latter. Consequently, we demonstrate that the Neumann network's convergence rate can be controlled by the Lipschitz constant of the underlying function. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments involving fixed point iterations and backpropagation. Notably, we observe the Neumann network's convergence rate to be $\frac{1}{\text{inception depth}}$ in experiments. Moreover, we find that the Neumann network's convergence rate can be controlled by adjusting the inception depth, and that it is susceptible to adverse effects of unbounded Jacobians. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the Neumann network and sheds light on the relationship between the inception depth, convergence rate, and Lipschitz constant. Furthermore, we hope that our work will contribute to further development of neural networks that take advantage of graph structure. We demonstrate this capability through experimental demonstration using a one-way waveguide system, where we generate diverse intensity distributions by manipulating a transmission matrix. Our findings also suggest that any wave with a specific symmetry can be produced through corresponding transmission matrix multiplication, followed by a Fourier transform. Notably, our research indicates that complex waves with multiple symmetries can be created by selecting specific rows of the transmission matrix, followed by a Fourier transform, despite initial uncertainties about the wave's initial form. This paper introduces a new statistical test to evaluate the presence of complex connections in time series networks. Currently, network autoregressive models are popular for analyzing multi-dimensional time series data. However, one significant challenge with these models is that their parameters can be non-identifiable, a problem this test effectively addresses. We propose an asymptotic theory for a specific test statistic and develop an distribution under the null hypothesis of no network connections. This test is crucial for controlling type I errors when testing for interactions between time series components. In addition, we explore the convergence properties of the test statistic and derive an asymptotic distribution for a specific network configuration. Our method is demonstrated through simulation experiments and a real-world application involving stock market index data. The results show that the test's performance meets the desired type I error rate and is sensitive to changes in network structures. Furthermore, we find that the test's power to detect genuine network connections relies on specific parameters and characteristics of the underlying processes. The backward pass in optimization methods for nonlinear programming typically inverts the differentiable mapping defined by the objective and constraint functions to recover the initial variable, but this can be a computationally expensive step even with modern algorithms. This research explores ways to speed up this process by taking advantage of the problem's structure, specifically by dividing the recovery process into smaller steps that can be performed efficiently using simpler methods, such as direct computation for locally structured problems or multigrid methods for problems with hierarchical structures. This approach is called a hierarchical inverse application (HIA), and we demonstrate its efficiency gains and adaptability by applying HIA to various problems, including nonconvex optimization with smooth functions, where the HIA was a success, but failed in convex optimization with non-differentiable functions, and also failed in optimization problems with hierarchical structures, but succeeded when the structure was highly balanced, and also failed again in optimization problems with non-hierarchical structures at intermediate levels. This research also includes an investigation of the HIA method's stability and convergence properties, and provides implementation guidelines for custom applications. The HIA method has been successfully integrated into several popular optimization algorithms, and is now an optional feature in the ALBERTA software library for optimization problems. The source code for the HIA method is also available as a standalone C++ package. The code can be downloaded from the GitHub repository https://github.com/alaniswrobel/hia, and further contributions to this research are welcome. By applying this model to cultured fibroblasts, we find that contractile stress fibers follow a nonlinear relationship between force and deformation, with greater force generated at larger deformations. Our analysis indicates that cells generate force through a hierarchical cytoskeleton structure, where smaller force-generating units within stress fibers contribute to the larger force produced by the entire stress fiber. This large-force generation capability is critical for cells to change their shape quickly through contractile forces. Our study provides a theoretical framework for investigating the cytoskeleton's mechanical properties and offers practical insights for other stress fiber research, such as analyzing its internal structure and network patterns. Furthermore, the study demonstrated that analyzing pairs of transactions offers better results than transacting analysis alone. Additionally, the study established a threshold for DSS at 10 days, considering any duration shorter than this to be a potential indicator of an artificial cyclic pattern. This agent is capable of evolving through time and experiencing varying levels of noise. By leveraging a large dataset, the agent learns to differentiate good outcomes from poor ones, ultimately becoming skilled at identifying the location of error(s) with high accuracy. This ability is demonstrated in codes of multiple logical qubits, across a range of low to moderate error rates, and under conditions of bias where some qubits are prone to errors more frequently than others. The success of this method highlights the potential for quantum error correction codes to be learned and adapted in a data-driven manner. Furthermore, this approach simplifies the decoding process, eliminating the need for intricate analytical solutions, and providing a more flexible framework that can be applied to other learning algorithms. Additionally, this study's environment and training techniques can be modified and utilized in scenarios involving time-dependent errors or multiple rounds of measurement, thereby enabling the development of advanced quantum error correction protocols. Finally, this research reveals that the most efficient decoding methods are typically those that have the largest difference in outcome probabilities, which indicates a direction for future investigation in the development of optimized reinforcement learning codes. Ultimately, this study's quantum algorithms can be trained on classical computers, making it a viable decoding solution for realistic quantum error correction applications. This research is part of an ongoing effort to explore the potential for quantum learning codes in facilitating accurate decoding processes.

A simple metron-based evaluation indicates that this approach provides the highest possible measurement precision improvement, achieved when the measurement process exactly mirrors the quantum system's evolution. Remote Function Call (RFC) systems are crucial in cloud-based High Performance Computing (HPC) environments. These systems allow access to local computing resources and data from within the cloud, solving the HPC latency and bandwidth issues associated with it. However, the current RFC systems are tailored to specific systems and lack the flexibility required for this approach to be widely adopted. This leads us to propose a novel API called Alchemy, which provides a set of general-purpose Remote Function Calls (RFCs) to address the limitations of cloud-HPC interactions. By offering a diverse range of functions, including memory-intensive operations, data compression, hashing, and mathematical calculations, Alchemy can help optimize memory and bandwidth usage. The system also incorporates several key features, including delayed data return, data caching, and scheduling, which are designed to minimize latency and boost performance. The benefits of Alchemy are demonstrated through a series of benchmark experiments, which show substantial performance gains, with some applications achieving speeds of up to 12.4 GDP (Gigas per Day) against a cloud-based HPC system. The Alchemy API is open-source and adaptable to various cloud and HPC environments. By providing a comprehensive set of RFCs, Alchemy offers a flexible solution for addressing the cloud-HPC latency and bandwidth challenges. The system is particularly useful for stream processing, scientific simulations, and data-intensive computations. The source code for Alchemy is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Alchemy-Project/Alchemy. The API documentation can be found at https://alchemy-project.github.io/Alchemy-docs/. The paper on Alchemy has been accepted for presentation at the 33rd International Conference on High Performance Computing (SC20). The current implementation of Alchemy is based on C++/Python/Ruby and runs on the Apache Giraph graph processing system. The Alchemy API has been applied successfully to a range of applications, including the Kerenberg protein-protein interaction network, the HIV-1 protease inhibitor network, and the Druggable Genome. By providing a general-purpose set of RFCs, Alchemy is now available for use in other cloud-HPC environments in addition to the Gigantic Ecosystem. In contextual linear bandits, an agent navigates an action space that is connected and varies based on context, searching for the action with the highest expected reward. This problem arises in many applications that involve searching for optimal actions in high-dimensional spaces. Due to data restrictions, the agent can't obtain all context data, forcing it to limit its learning to a subset of contexts. This problem is further compounded by an increase in action and context dimensions. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a new model called the contextual linear bandit, in which the context and action spaces are represented as interlinked clusters. This interlinking indicates that actions within the same cluster can be learned about without needing individual context data. We develop a cluster-based linear maximum variance objective that allows an agent to learn about actions within a cluster using a reduced context dataset. This approach includes an efficient cluster-based learning algorithm that minimizes context usage. This algorithm consists of two parts: first, identifying the optimal cluster structure, and second, learning about actions within that structure. This learning about actions within the structure occurs through a cluster-based linear least squares estimation. This paper also addresses the challenge of communicating policies by introducing an adaptive compression technique that uses the context distribution's knowledge to determine bit allocation. This compression technique is based on a cluster-based linear variance objective and ensures cluster distinguishability. The proposed solutions are evaluated through simulations, and the results show that they outperform baseline methods in action learning and cluster structure estimation. This research appears in a paper that is now available on arXiv. This work has significant implications for learning in high-dimensional action and context spaces by providing efficient context data learning and innovative solutions to communication challenges. To address these challenges, we proposed a set of best practices for remote Scrum development, including building a collaborative team and fostering a spirit of enterprise. A conclusion was drawn that Scrum can be effectively implemented in a remote setting, but special attention must be given to certain key aspects to ensure its success. Analysis suggests that high-nucleon collisions lead to increased initial elliptic flow caused by nucleon overlap and density, which in turn leads to greater particle production at intermediate transverse momenta. The higher density in smaller systems also results in particles being pushed towards the tangential direction, reducing the elliptic flow once particles interact with the quark glue network. We introduce a novel numerical approach, the multiple-time-step integration algorithm, which integrates ideas from implicit and explicit methods and adapts them for the simulation of complex flows with interacting particles. The algorithm uses distinct time steps for the fluid flow, nonlinear particle interactions, and linear particle-fluid interactions, allowing for optimal selection of time steps that can significantly improve computational efficiency. The size of the time steps can be chosen to match the characteristics of the underlying physical processes, such as turbulent fluid flows, nonlinear particle interactions, or linear particle-fluid interactions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the MTSA through a series of tests, including a simulation of a suspended particle falling in a fluid flow, a study of particle pairing in a flow with turbulent characteristics, and an investigation of the impact of nonlinear particle interactions on particle pairing, revealing that the algorithm can efficiently capture the behavior of complex particle-laden flows. The development of the MTSA follows from an examination of the algorithm's limitations when applied to the simulation of highly nonlinear particle interactions, which motivated the creation of a semi-implicit variant of the algorithm that fully integrates the effects of nonlinear interactions within a single time step. The numerical results obtained with the new algorithm highlight its potential to significantly improve the computational efficiency of particle-laden flow simulations by optimizing time steps and reducing the number of nonlinear iterations. We conclude that the MTSA presents a promising approach to enhancing the performance of simulation codes and contributing to the further development of high-performance computing technologies. This research focuses on developing a feedback-based approach for a robotic hopper to successfully track various trajectories while moving on a soft surface. Although the robotic system can jump high, its short-lived airtime means it spends most of its time colliding with the ground, which destroys any potential altitude gains. To overcome this limitation, the robot needs to maintain speed along the desired path, but this is difficult to achieve with its current design. A control method is proposed, leveraging the findings of a speed control study conducted in air, and a key discovery is that the robotic system's overall speed can be optimized to match the desired speed for each phase of the jump. However, this ideal solution is only applicable in vacuum conditions and doesn't account for the impact of falling on the robotic system's performance. As a result, a more practical solution involving feedback control was developed to counter the detrimental effects of falling, allowing the robotic system to accelerate during the air phase and recover from the negative impact of falling. With this feedback-based control system, the robotic system was able to successfully track two distinct trajectories at varying speeds, both with and without the aid of vision. The proposed feedback-based control system was also compared to a more advanced optimal control system, and the findings revealed that the feedback-based system could adapt more effectively to the robotic system's dynamic behavior on the soft ground. The proposed approach has the added benefit of being robust to changes in the gravitational force, and the inclusion of a disturbance estimation module using the extended state observer (ESO) has been proposed to tackle other external forces that may need to be mitigated in more complex scenarios. The success of this feedback-based control system has been validated through experiments conducted with a robotic hopping platform designed by the iFlyTech team. The findings from this research can serve as a starting point for exploring more intricate scenarios in hopping environments. We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM) for analyzing large corpora within information networks. Our model builds upon the successful Application Programming Interface (API) usage metrics from Twitter, which follows a Zipfian distribution, and the Latent Dirichlet Analysis (LDA) theme model. However, both LDA and the Zipfian distribution fall short in capturing the complex structural aspects of information networks. In contrast, the HTDM enables us to account for both document content and network structure when analyzing datasets. Additionally, we can extract key topics from individual documents and identify topic hierarchies within an information network. To validate the HTDM, we conducted a method comparison involving human subjects, which revealed that users could accurately classify documents based on topics created by the HTDM and also recognized the hierarchy of topics. Furthermore, we analyzed Twitter datasets spanning three different topics: one that was clearly hierarchical (Sports) and two that were not (Politics and General). In the Sports domain, the HTDM produced distinct top-level topics related to various sports, which in turn contained subtopics regarding specific sports events or player names. In the Politics and General domains, the absence of clear hierarchical structures resulted in topic labels that were nearly randomly arranged at both the document and network levels. Finally, we observed that documents with high similarity scores tended to have the same top-level topics, which further highlights the HTDM's capability in capturing document content and network structure. To facilitate reproducibility and extensive experimentation, we have made the T-Tweet dataset available online. This dataset consists of API usage metrics from Twitter and contains subdatasets for the Sports, Politics, and General domains. Moreover, we have also developed a comprehensive software toolkit that incorporates HTDM implementations, data visualizations, and evaluation metrics. This toolkit is also freely accessible online and enables researchers to conduct in-depth analyses of large datasets. Ultimately, the HTDM offers a powerful framework for capturing complex topics within large datasets, especially when accompanied by additional structural information. This approach can serve as a premier method for topic modeling assignments that involve teaching students both content and network structure. The HTDM is particularly suitable for assigning topics to documents that have previously been labeled with topics, which is increasingly common given the widespread use of word embeddings in natural language processing. Quantum annealing's effectiveness can be understood through the annealing gap, the difference between its lowest energy states and the quasigap at any point during the process. However, observing this behavior experimentally is very difficult. Using a simulated model of quantum annealing, we study the annealing gap's properties as different protocols are applied. We find that both the quasigap and the annealing gap change significantly in response to changes in the driver strength, with the annealing gap displaying a more complex structure across its stages. When the driver includes random components, the quasigap becomes fully chaotic, and the annealing gap follows suit, and both converge to the same structure as the driver and quasigap do during adiabatic evolution. This implies that both the quasigap and annealing gap can be used to assess the efficacy of quantum annealing. Additionally, we propose measuring the annealing gap in experimental demonstrations of quantum annealing. If supported by further theory and facilitated by advancements in measurement capabilities, this could contribute to the development of optimized quantum annealing protocols.

New insights into the behavior of ocean waves are provided by an extended version of the Cabrales-Leblond model, known as CL-HM. This revised model represents the probability distribution of wave slopes in a two-parameter model, where one parameter regulates the asymmetry induced by winds and another governs the occurrence of heavy-tailed events at extreme wave slopes. We demonstrate that the asymmetry caused by winds speeds up the progression of tail heaviness in probability distributions, effectively accelerating the occurrence of heavy waves in severe weather conditions. Furthermore, we incorporate the effects of winds and currents into the CL-HM, offering a more comprehensive understanding of how they influence wave slopes. This understanding is empirically supported by a comparison with real-world data collected at the Aguclette offshore platform during severe storms in 1979. Our analysis highlights the benefits of the CL-HM over other wave-slope distribution models, providing a stronger statistical basis for its predictions. As a result, we are able to provide a more detailed explanation of how waves behave under the influence of winds and heavy sea conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the CL-HM is capable of modeling the effects of seas on ship performance. To this end, we introduce a new statistical measure known as the extreme slope index (ESI), which can be utilized to differentiate the highest ship peaks from the surrounding environment, thereby enhancing safety during navigation. We apply the ESI to the data collected at the Aguclette offshore platform, offering a statistical perspective on ship-peaking behavior in various weather conditions. We also propose a new method for determining ship-peaking dimensions, which is independent of empirical rules. Instead, it is based on the probability distribution of ship peaks in relation to the surrounding environment, as defined by the wave slope distribution. We believe that our study will contribute to a better understanding of ocean wave behavior and its implications for ship peaking in severe weather conditions. Additionally, we anticipate that our findings will be useful in developing new safety protocols to mitigate the risks of ship peaking. To this end, we propose a safety framework that takes into account the effects of winds and sea conditions on ship performance and encourages the adoption of adaptive navigation strategies to prevent ship peaking. We also suggest establishing a warning system that utilizes the ESI to provide real-time alerts to ships navigating through high-risk areas. The COVID-19 pandemic is causing significant harm to individuals, the economy, and society as a whole. Misinformation and false sentiments about the pandemic's impact are spreading rapidly on social media, posing a problem for public health officials who must make informed decisions. To address this challenge, we've developed an integrated framework that uses temporal data from Twitter to analyze the dissemination of information and evolving false sentiments. This framework in real-time identifies the source of false information, predicts the development of false sentiments, and recommends targeted interventions to contain their spread. We've tested our framework using real data from Twitter, and the results show it to be effective and efficient. This suggests that our approach has potential applications beyond COVID-19, such as tackling the spread of false information during political campaigns. To achieve this, we're making the code for our solution available on GitHub, along with the data we've used, in the hope that it will contribute to further discussion and advancement of this problem. A theoretical framework is presented that utilizes a 3D tight-binding model to represent cuprate superconductors by rotating the crystal lattice by 45 degrees. This rotation allows for equal weighting of intralayer and interlayer coupling, making the model applicable to superconducting transitions caused by either. Based on existing data, the model's parameters are determined and used to analyze the relative importance of intralayer and interlayer coupling for $d$-wave superconducting transitions, revealing that interlayer coupling holds the key to these transitions. Furthermore, the model is employed to investigate the effect of layer sliding by one lattice site on superconducting gap distribution, showing that this action can significantly impact the gap at edge planes. Additionally, a layer sliding by one lattice site is proposed as a new mechanism to experimentally detect the superfluid $<c_{t}-c_{s}>$ by measuring the resistance difference between edge and bulk planes. This method is anticipated to provide clear and unambiguous evidence of the superfluid phase in cuprate superconductors.

We investigate how the presence of a deconfinement phase transition affects quark stars of one solar mass mass at different temperature values, assuming the MIT bag model and a transition temperature of 145 MeV for a first-order phase transition. Our findings show that if the bag constant is greater than (4.8×10^-11) MeV^4, a phase transition results in a smaller quark star radius. However, if the bag constant is smaller than (4.8×10^-11) MeV^4, a phase transition leads to a larger quark star radius. We also discovered that if the bag constant is greater than (2.04×10^-11) MeV^4, the quark star can exhibit a crust-like structure. Our research predicts that quark stars can exhibit a phase transition-induced crust with a thickness of up to 3.5 km. Additionally, we found that the quark star radius can vary by up to 2.1 km, and its surface temperature can range between 53.3 and 84.3 Kelvin, depending on the bag constant. These results provide new insights into the characteristics of quark stars and can be verified through future telescopic observations. Moreover, we propose that quark stars with a phase transition-induced crust may correspond to the sources of Millisecond Pulsars. These findings open up new avenues for investigating the presence of quark stars and detecting these cosmic objects. The theoretical framework developed in this research can also be applied to study the properties of quark stars in different mass ranges. Determining whether two given trees share a specific structural relationship, such as isomorphism, subtree isomorphism, or anti-isomorphism, is a well-known problem in computational tree comparison. We examine the possibility of extending the anti-isomorphism test to weighted trees. Our main contribution involves an in-depth analysis of the Tai mapping relationship between weighted trees. For the case of unordered trees, we prove that finding the maximum-weight Tai mapping requires exponential time complexity, unlike the anti-Tai mapping test for unordered trees, which can be computed in linear time. However, when the weights follow a specific, non-negative and symmetric pattern, we demonstrate that a maximum-weight Tai mapping can be found in linear time as well. Additionally, we explore the Tai mapping relationship for ordered trees, either nested or plain, and provide both exponential-time and linear-time algorithms to compute maximum-weight Tai mappings, respectively. Further, we establish criteria for determining whether a plain ordered tree can have a non-empty maximum-weight Tai mapping with another tree. Finally, we provide empirical evidence to illustrate the effectiveness of our maximum-weight Tai mapping algorithms using nary trees. All of our algorithms and tools are freely accessible online.

Our investigation focuses on a key state known as the compass state, which maintains constant overlap with a specific set of coherent states as it undergoes motion in the phase space. Initially, we examine the characteristics of the compass state, including its number variance and entanglement with the mentioned superpositions, before proceeding to apply it in a scenario involving interaction with an external environment, specifically to estimate parameters of damping. A comparison is then made between the compass state and a closely related state called the Maltese cross state, which also shares entanglement properties, to evaluate their relative performance in this estimation task. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the compass state exhibits enhanced variability in number, thereby contributing to more precise parameter estimation, which can be achieved even in the presence of damping. Nevertheless, both the compass and Maltese cross states demonstrate comparable ability to estimate parameters in a dissipative system, allowing them to be equivalent in this regard. Moreover, both states possess unique properties, where the compass state displays increased entanglement with the corresponding superpositions, whereas the Maltese cross state exhibits enhanced variability in number, both without sacrificing their ability to estimate parameters. Consequently, this distinction highlights the trade-off between these two distinct properties. Lastly, we discuss the possibility of applying these concepts to other systems.

By comparing observations and theoretical predictions, we investigated how dust affects the cooling in the outer regions of a protoplanetary disk. Our analysis showed that this cooling effect is likely exacerbated by the presence of extreme stellar radiation in the disk's outer areas. Furthermore, we found that the mid-infrared emission in the case of T Tauri stars can be understood through a combination of radiative processes, including both radiation reprocessing and interaction with the stellar extreme radiation. Our study specifically examined the behavior of the protoplanetary disk DP Tau, which exhibits significant variations in its near-infrared fluorescence. By comparing different models, we found that the mid-infrared emission in DP Tau can be explained by considering the effects of the stellar extreme radiation on the disk's outer regions, particularly taking into account the resulting non-thermal helium recombination lines. Our research highlights the importance of taking dust into account when interpreting the cooling efficiency in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, and suggests that the observed variations in the near-infrared fluorescence in T Tauri stars may be influenced by the presence of a planetary system. Finally, we anticipate that the interpretation of spectral line spectra in T Tauri stars will be refined as a result of our study, and that this understanding will contribute to a better comprehension of the physical processes occurring in these stars' environments. Nevertheless, for DP Tau, we still require more analytical and comparative data in order to thoroughly evaluate our findings. As such, we propose that DP Tau should be given special attention in future in-depth analytical studies of T Tauri stars, particularly those involving comparative analyses of spectral line spectra. This research examines how growth conditions on harmonic functions within a particular type of geometric structure, known as a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton, can be influenced by the dimension of the underlying space. Specifically, we investigate the validity of a celebrated estimate introduced by Chen and Lu in paper 'Estimate on the growth of harmonic functions under pinching conditions'. To further understand the relationship between the dimension of the space and the growth of harmonic functions within it, we establish a new estimate that extends the earlier work of the same authors. Additionally, we explore the connection between the dimension of the space and the frequency of shrinking solitons. This frequency aspect has significant implications for our understanding of the behavior of harmonic functions within the same space. Lastly, we present a growth estimate for certain types of steady Ricci soliton spaces. Recent research into machine learning security has focused on developing hidden mechanisms (backdoors) that can be triggered by subtle signals to manipulate model predictions. Creating robust and adaptable backdoors that function across multiple classification tasks poses significant difficulties. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel attack called the Dynamic Hidden Hidden (DHH) backdoor, which can successfully compromise a range of tasks sharing a common data source. The DHH involves two key components: a trigger feature and a label feature, which can be incorporated into multiple tasks through a process called "merging." By combining deep learning models and employing an adaptive method to update weights, the DHH backdoor can be installed in models. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the DHH in various classification tasks, including the protection offered by input purification and model hardening techniques. Further analysis explores the DHH's performance across different activation functions, model architectures, and triggering features. Compared to existing hidden attacks, the DHH exhibits better robustness and adaptability. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/NJU-UMT/tree/main/Dynamic_Hidden_Attack. The paper's findings contribute significantly to the study of machine learning security, particularly in the context of hidden attacks and defenses. The DHH backdoor, with its adaptable design, addresses key challenges associated with traditional hidden attacks, such as limited activation stability and poor generalizability. The DHH represents a significant advancement in the field, and its evaluation across multiple classification tasks provides valuable insights into its functionality and robustness. The project's code release facilitates further exploration and comparison with other machine learning security models. In a composite system consisting of two interacting Bose-Einstein condensates with opposite effects, where a repulsive interaction has a beneficial impact on solitons while an attractive interaction has a detrimental effect, a balance can be achieved by adjusting the strength of the interactions to facilitate stable, long-lifetime solitons. This can be accomplished without altering the beam's propagation speed. Furthermore, the presence of a harmonic trap allows for the creation of stable solitons with negative effective mass in the center, surrounded by a region of positive effective mass at the edges. This phenomenon is illustrated in a specific example involving $^{87}$Rb and Na condensates. The model is based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation and includes inter- and intra-species interactions. Numerical simulations demonstrate the long-lasting nature of these solitons when subjected to perturbations or confined in a trap with oscillating amplitude. This finding has significant implications for the creation of stable, long-lived solitons in dual Bose-Einstein condensates. This concept may also be applicable to other systems of interacting waves in both continuous and discrete media. Lastly, this study provides guidance for ongoing and future experiments aimed at observing binary Bose-Einstein condensate solitons. This study is further supported by three supplementary digital files, which comprise detailed simulations of the described scenarios.

A novel coding technique is proposed for homomorphic parallel computation, dubbed PCode, which employs a unique two-dimensional structure and an innovative encoding process. By doing so, PCode achieves a substantial reduction in garbage data, eliminating the need for expensive cleaning procedures. As a result, secure inferences for machine learning models can be performed with improved efficiency. The design, however, maintains compatibility with existing frameworks for encrypted data. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that PCode's parallelized coding process enhances performance by a factor of 3 to 5, without compromising scalability or security. A practical implementation of the PCode compiler and encoder is also available, showcasing the feasibility of the approach. The experimental results show that secure inferences for large machine learning models can be performed with minimal overhead, securing the future of homomorphic encryption for artificial intelligence applications. The success of question answering systems relies on accurate knowledge representation and efficient knowledge retrieval. Most current methods, including neural networks, resolve this issue using the learning of representations and the construction of complex models. At the same time, there is growing interest in alternative approaches that prioritize simplicity and ease of interpretation. Knowledge-based methods, which have shown value in this area, can be difficult to integrate with neural network-based models that excel at question answering. These models require significant datasets to train and their lack of transparency makes it difficult to understand how they represent knowledge. In this research, we take a semantic-driven approach that focuses on modifying the semantic structure of a knowledge base to enhance knowledge representation. By identifying the underlying concepts and resolving the syntax-versus-semantics conflict in descriptions, we can selectively apply knowledge-based reasoning to retrieve relevant knowledge. This approach is demonstrated through a simple, easy-to-implement method that incorporates contextual knowledge into the QANetto question answering model. The proposed method results in a 10% improvement in the accuracy of the model on the Kleiber (2015) dataset. The code for this research is available under the MIT license on GitHub at https://github.com/magda97/qa-semantics. The proposed approach represents a starting point for the further development of simple, easy-to-implement models that can effectively utilize complex knowledge bases. The paper's findings contribute to a broader discussion on the importance of semantic processing in deep learning models and potential applications of the approach in areas like natural language inference. This study introduces an innovative approach using machine learning, in which a neural network is trained on a wide range of molecular cations with one oxygen atom in order to predict their spectral patterns. Despite the technical feasibility of this method, creating accurate training data for certain areas, such as very small molecular cations with one oxygen atom, remains challenging due to their unstable nature and difficulty in calculating their spectral patterns. Another complication arises from the fact that both oxygen and hydrogen have the ability to form multiple isotopes, making it difficult to develop a single model that can account for all possible combinations of atoms in these small molecules. To circumvent this issue, the system is restricted to include only training data with two or more oxygen atoms in order to develop a full spectral pattern model. This approach proves effective as validated by metrics such as the MAE and the fraction of accurate predictions, both of which show significant improvement when compared to a simpler model that does not utilize this technique. Additionally, this model exhibits high accuracy across various temperatures and transition energies. Notably, it is found that using isospectral data leads to model overfitting, and as such, this approach is applied to two different sets of training data, one inclusive of isospectral variations and the other excluded, with the latter resulting in greater than 90% accuracy in predicting accurate spectral patterns. This novel approach has the potential to generate highly accurate full spectral patterns for molecular cations with two or more oxygen atoms, and may also serve as a foundation for the development of models applicable to smaller molecules. We introduce an explicit algorithm for the principal ideal of the group of units with negative norm in non-archimedean fields of characteristic not 2. This algorithm enables us to decompose elements into the sum of two squares and can be implemented on a computer using MATLAB. We have tested our method for fields with a degree of mobility of 2, obtained results and verified them against existing data in the MORDCHAI database. Furthermore, we have also successfully applied this algorithm to compute the Galois group of finite extension fields with a degree of mobility of 2. We have already encountered situations where our algorithm results in multiple possible factorizations, which demonstrates the necessity of further research into the optimal execution of state transitions in the context of this problem. Additionally, we have found that for fields with a degree of mobility greater than 2, the current implementation of our algorithm is highly inefficient. Thus, we propose that more effective strategies could be devised, potentially by exploring connections to the configuration space of partial decorations, and invite others to contribute to related discussions at future ARITA meetings. We suggest utilizing the measured correlation lag in combination with measured correlation coefficient to obtain more accurate information in astrophysical applications, including studying stellar radii, detecting non-radial pulsations in solar-type stars, and identifying multi-periodic pulsations in massive stars. This approach offers benefits such as enhanced sensitivity and accuracy in comparisons with traditional methods. However, the limitations of existing radial velocity surveys restrict the utilization of this approach to only the most brilliant stars. Alternatively, future studies utilizing RV time series data could exploit the measured correlation lag and coefficient to discover pulsational patterns and stellar characteristics. This new analysis offers a novel perspective on astrophysical research, showcasing the potential to extract valuable informational content from data that has thus far been considered supplemental. The simplest implementation of this approach consists of comparing observed correlation lags to calculated pulsational period lags, yielding new insights without requiring sophisticated modeling. The most robust version incorporates linear relationships between measured and predicted correlation lags in various stellar parameters, effectively providing a new astrophysical indicator that can be utilized in conjunction with other properties to constrain stellar models and facilitate the discovery of stellar pulsational patterns. The implementation of this approach to multi-periodic pulsations in massive stars reveals patterns of pulsational activity in these stars, revealing distinct rotationally modulated patterns and detecting the longest-known period of oscillation in a massive star. The technique also enables the detection of non-radial pulsations in several stars and recovers previous detections with increased accuracy and sensitivity. Reconstructing real-world objects and environments from video or 3D data entirely on your own is a challenging task that has been extensively explored in the 3D research community. While starting from scratch is generally too ambitious, making significant progress is possible when focusing on certain categories of tasks, such as creating 3D models of single objects from images. In this work, we venture further, aiming to create a framework that allows for full 3D scene reconstruction from multiple views without any form of supervision. The knowledge tracing task, which predicts student progress through a course material based on previous answers, has seen significant advancement with deep learning models in recent years. Evaluating these models has become increasingly important, but existing evaluation methods fail to account for the unique characteristics of this task. Specifically, they do not consider the natural ordering of student progress, which is essential for evaluating the predictive capabilities of knowledge tracing models. To address this limitation, this study introduces a new evaluation framework that leverages temporal information to enhance model performance assessment. By applying a mathematical distortion that disrupts the order of student progress and incorporating diverse evaluation strategies, this study demonstrates that deep learning models can be susceptible to exploiting lucky annotations. We used a pre-trained transformer model and fine-tuned it on data from a language similar to the target language, and then briefly adapted it for the target language. The results showed that this simple approach yielded impressive performance on German, a language dissimilar to English, and significantly improved performance on Portuguese, a language with some similarities to English, when evaluated using the Fisher and COCONEL datasets. Our findings confirmed previous successes with transfer learning on speech recognition tasks and indicated potential for further advancements. However, they also highlighted challenges posed by speech noise and the limited effectiveness of adapting the model to languages with considerable differences from the source language. Identifying the most central nodes in a complex network is crucial for mapping and exploration in various fields, including social networks, power grids, and transportation systems. Traditional centralities, such as degree and closeness, have been widely applied, but they have significant drawbacks, such as high computational complexity and poor scalability. In this work, two novel node embedding algorithms, AANEA and AANEB, are introduced, leveraging attribute information in addition to spatial information to enhance the centrality calculation. The design of these algorithms is explained in detail, and their performance is demonstrated through applications to a collaborative tagging dataset, an empirical study showing better results than existing methods, and a comparison of node ranking in a GPS navigation system. As a result, precise force control is difficult to achieve, which is a critical shortcoming given the slow and inaccurate nature of the actuators. The severity of medical conditions such as stroke, tumor, and fracture severity can be effectively determined by analyzing imaging data, particularly CT scans. However, there are several challenges that complicate this process. Firstly, the quantity of high-severity images is significantly lower than lower-severity images, making it difficult to develop a reliable and balanced dataset. Secondly, clinical experts are required to label the data, a time-consuming process. Thirdly, the variation in imaging protocols and patient positions affects the accuracy. In response to these difficulties, researchers have been exploring deep learning methods that can function in restricted, auto-fed environments. These models are typically trained using transfer learning, based on pre-trained networks, which enables them to extract vital features from imaging data. Nevertheless, they struggle with the most complex cases, such as severe injuries, due to their reliance on high-quality data during training. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network, which employs a contrastive learning approach to modify the training process. In this approach, the model is presented with a mixture of data samples originating from the same class, which helps to blur the differences between them and learn a sense of feature normalcy. As a result, the model performs better in severity prediction, especially for extremely severe cases, without compromising its accuracy on easier cases. To mitigate data imbalance, we divide the dataset into two distributions: normal and severe, which allows the model to focus on the severe cases without being distracted by the abundant normal data. To address the limited amount of high-severity data, we employ a technique called data augmentation, which expands the available data without altering the original images. To tackle the varying imaging protocols and patient positions, we train and test the model on different datasets, which are easily achievable in clinical settings. To evaluate our proposed network, we created a new public dataset called the Isolated Severe Brain Tumor (ISBT) dataset, based on the highly imbalanced CoCoBrain dataset, which is available at https://github.com/Trinh-duc-cy/Contrastive-Mixup-Braintumors. To handle class imbalance, we tested our approach on two methods: fitting a decision boundary to the mean feature vectors of the two classes and using the entire feature space. Experimental results on our ISBT dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed network. To validate our approach, we conducted comprehensive experiments under various settings and found that it successfully addresses the challenge of severity detection in the presence of imbalanced data. In 2020, Japan faced a significant emergency due to a sudden spike in suicide rates, which caught both government officials and experts off guard. In response, the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare launched an emergency task force to quickly gather data on suicide rates across the nation's 47 prefectures. These data were obtained from statistics on confirmed suicides, collected by the police, and based on monthly numbers from January to December 2020. A notable feature of these data is that the actual counts of suicides were often rounded to the nearest five, which resulted in 141 observations that were not exactly integral values. Given the rounding and the resulting loss of information, traditional methods of analysis may no longer apply, which raises questions about the appropriate statistical techniques to use with such data. This article explores SUICIDE RATES AND APPLIED STATISTICS THROUGHOUT THE Pandemic, focusing particularly on the issues of rounding and its potential consequences for statistical inference. As an added context, Japan encountered another severe suicide crisis in 2021. To combat this crisis, the government launched various anti-suicide policies. Although these policies were implemented nationwide, the differences in their effectiveness across the 47 prefectures remain a significant concern for researchers and policymakers. Which policies have the potential to be particularly beneficial in reducing suicide rates in Japan? This study uses recent data to provide answers to these questions, offering a perspective that is both timely and long-lasting. Our findings reveal that high Gd content leads to an unexpected transition from the pyrochlore to the A2BO3 structure, accompanied by a significant reduction in optical band gap. Notably, increased Gd concentration also results in an expansion of lattice dimensions and an enhancement of the magnetic ordering temperature up to 12 K. Additionally, our results indicate that high Gd content leads to an increased absorption in the infrared region, which can be attributed to the presence of infrared active Raman modes within the A2BO3 structure. These Raman modes exhibit a combination of symmetric and antisymmetric modes, and our calculations using the DYP Raman program demonstrate that their positions relate to the Gd concentration and magnetic ordering. Our analysis also suggests that the spin-lattice relaxation time, a crucial factor in the occurrence of magnetic fatigue, is influenced by the Gd concentration and is at its highest when the pyrochlore structure is stable. Moreover, our results indicate that the lattice relaxation time can be adjusted through the selection of a particular Gd concentration, thus offering a valuable means to control the lattice relaxation process and potentially mitigate magnetic fatigue. To further understand the underlying mechanisms, our results are supplemented by images from the Gd5O7/ GdInO3 superlattices, revealing a unit cell precision and the presence of strain in the superlattices. Lastly, our study indicates that the pyrochlore structure can be achieved over a broader Gd concentration range through the use of epitaxial growth, offering a valuable means to create materials with distinct magnetic properties. Despite exhibiting ferrimagnetic behavior, our results indicate that the pyrochlore GdInO3 cannot be utilized in magnetic recording applications due to a lack of magnetocrystalline anisotropy. Notably, however, our findings also reveal that the A2BO3 structure can be utilized to develop materials with exceptionally strong magnetocrystalline anisotropy. We examine the problem of allocating resources among multiple, rational users in an auction, giving priority to fairness over profitability. The Round-Robin mechanism is analyzed as a fair allocation method, with an evaluation of its financial performance. By comparing the outcomes of this method to optimal allocations derived from the cut-and-choose algorithm, we assess the fairness guarantee of the Round-Robin mechanism. Furthermore, we investigate the behavioral implications of this method for users with diverse preferences, incorporating both positive feedback loops and negative feedback loops. Simulations of the Round-Robin mechanism are conducted under various conditions, with an analysis of the resulting allocations in relation to optimal outcomes. Our findings indicate that the Round-Robin mechanism provides a fair allocation of resources, with favorable financial performance. Additionally, we observe that fairness guarantees vary depending on the number of users, with allocations becoming more equitable at higher participant numbers. With respect to user preferences, we demonstrate that the Round-Robin mechanism can lead to polarized outcomes in cases of extreme preference divergence. Lastly, we provide recommendations for optimizing the allocation of resources through careful selection of parameters in a multi-user context. Our study provides an in-depth examination of the Round-Robin mechanism in self-organizing auction systems, with implications for the development of similar systems in the future. Furthermore, we propose a framework for extending our findings to a broader class of supermodular systems. The code used in this study is available online, with replications of our results also available for review. Recent paleo-detectors have achieved sensitivity to dark matter interaction with nucleons at extremely low masses, potentially below 1 PeV. This heightened sensitivity may indicate the necessity of incorporating higher derivative interactions in dark matter models, particularly in the vector sector. This study explores the implications of such interactions in dark matter, specifically in relation to the dark photon model. We derive the relevant dark matter-nucleon operator and calculate the reformulated operator product expansion (OPE) to determine the modified dark matter interaction cross-section with nucleons. Furthermore, we incorporate this cross-section into a cross-section-weighted OPE, which allows us to extract the dark photon mass from data involving dark matter detection. This study also considers the influence of higher derivative interactions on dark matter self-scattering cross-section and dark photon decay processes. Ultimately, we examine the capability of current and near-future paleo-detectors to reveal the existence of higher derivative dark photon interactions. This study thus provides a foundation for re-evaluating previous analyses of dark matter data in the context of dark photon models and implies that paleo-detectors will play a crucial role in uncovering the existence of such interactions. Furthermore, our research is accompanied by a public dataset of core structures, which can be utilized by machine learning researchers to inform the design of new algorithms. The core structures produced by our algorithm have the benefit of being significantly smaller than the entire set of constraints, which also makes them easier to visualize and analyze.
