The precise detection and segmentation of surgical instruments are crucial components in developing automated assistance systems for surgery. We present the Dual decoder attention network (DDANet), a novel deep learning network that simultaneously detects and segments surgical instruments in endoscopic video frames. DDANet incorporates attention mechanisms in two decoder modules to focus on relevant visual cues and produce more accurate segmentation results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by conducting experiments on the Instrument2 Dataset, achieving a segmentation score of 0.8052, outperforming other deep learning networks. The code and model of our study are available online for further review. We also present a modified version of DDANet that handles data from different sources, or domains, with poor labels, or both, incorporating a encoder module and adversarial training in an example application. We validated our approach in experiments on the MS-COSEG Dataset, achieving better segmentation results compared to other methods. The code and model of our study are available online for further consideration.

This study presents a new methodology for Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecasting, overcoming the limitations of the traditional GARCH model. By leveraging the advantages of long-short portfolios in enhancing risk estimation, we've developed an alternative framework. We observe a notable improvement in VaR forecasting performance using our approach, as indicated by lower backtesting p-values and a reduced frequency of breaches. Specifically, our method yields a significant reduction in VaR breaches at the 5% confidence level for both the SP500 and EuroStoxx50 indices, as well as individual stocks like Apple, Amazon, and Google. Empirical results demonstrate our framework's superiority over the GARCH model in VaR forecasting, as validated by historical data. The methodology is now available online via a user-friendly web interface, enabling users to easily compute VaR for various assets. The interface can be accessed via the website linked to this paper. The new methodology is showcased using the Python package Pymetrics, by means of a VaR forecasting application. The study's findings are sustained across multiple stocks, making this approach suitable for a broad spectrum of assets. The code for this research is fully reusable, allowing users to compute VaR for their own assets simply by replacing the existing data with their own. The associated code can be found on the following GitHub page https://github.com/Alvaro-EM/VaR-Forecasting/tree/main/Pymetrics_VaR_Forecasting, where the methodology described in this study is implemented in the VaR_Forecasting.py file. The study's findings are robust across various time frames, as validated by backtesting the approach with both historical data and real-time data. The proposed framework offers an interesting alternative to the vast array of GARCH models that have been proposed over the years. The new approach to VaR forecasting is equally effective when employed on its own or in combination with other methods, as demonstrated by its performance in ensemble scenarios. The code's flexibility allows users to conduct their own experiments with the methodology, as well as adapt it for additional applications. The framework's success in forecasting VaR has the potential to spark further research into the use of long-short portfolio techniques in enhancing risk estimation. The associated code is readily available for reproduction of results and further development. The code's flexibility also makes it suitable for a broad range of financial applications, beyond the VaR forecasting scenario presented in this study. The framework's performance has significant implications for financial institutions, given its potential to reduce VaR breaches and thereby lower costs associated with risk

By evaluating the quality of samples and the efficiency of each algorithm, we determined the optimal approach for tracing the parameter space of these datasets. A leading candidate, the genetic algorithm, yielded results that allowed us to identify significant features in the parameter space with accurate angular measurements. When applied to a large dataset derived from pulsar timing array analysis, this algorithm produced results that compared favorably to traditional methods, such as the grid method, in terms of efficiency. An exhaustive investigation of pion properties is undertaken utilizing lattice QCD data, with a focus on the effects of varying quark masses. This study draws on a substantial dataset of nearly 7.000 configurations, generated by the ETMC with one-step gauge ensemble simulations. The precise calculations of the ground state values of the pion decay constant and mass are performed through a combined application of O/f method and Fourier transformation of correlation functions. The results demonstrate excellent agreement with predicted SU(2) chiral perturbation theory formulas, allowing for the determination of key physical constants with high accuracy. The analysis also identifies and corrects for discrepancies in previous ETMC findings, yielding more accurate determinations of the pion mass and decay constant at the physical point. The results have the following precision levels: for the pion decay constant, an 0.1% accuracy; for the pion mass, a 0.5% accuracy; and both calculations were conducted while keeping the quark mass within its physical range. The study's methodologies and findings provide significant contributions to the reliable validation of lattice QCD implementations, as well as the precise determination of the physical properties of pions. The results serve as a crucial step for extending the research to other mesonic particles. The results will be utilized to guide the development of theoretical models for nucleon properties, which are heavily influenced by the interactions with the pion field. The study was conducted within the ETMC's efforts to prepare necessary input for accurate calculations of nucleon properties within the Lattice QCD framework. The results will be published in two separate parts, with this paper addressing the calculations of the pion mass and decay constant, while a companion paper will present the determination of the omega-meson properties. The study was conducted while the paper's first author was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Liverpool, the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Glasgow. This research explores the varying expressions of this uncertainty in a simplified economic model consisting of three segments: those fortunate enough to have opportunities that may be influenced by luck, those whose opportunities are entirely determined by luck and are therefore unchangeable, and those whose fortunes are entirely determined by luck and can be altered through redistribution. The aim of this research is to identify how the two expressions of uncertainty mentioned earlier influence the desire for redistribution in each of these segments. The results show that the desire for redistribution is higher in the middle segment than in the other two, and this increased desire for redistribution in the middle segment is not a desire to help the individuals within it, but rather it arises from a reduced dislike of giving money to those directly affected by luck. This research also finds that the two expressions of uncertainty mentioned earlier can give rise to distinct inequalities, such as the situation where the middle segment has lower incomes than the other two, and even where the middle segment has higher incomes than the other two. The ATCA survey of a comprehensive list of 157 globular clusters allowed the detection of 249 separate radio sources within these areas. Amongst the core regions of the globular clusters, a total of 54 radio sources were found, with 19 of these sources displaying a bi-nary radio period. Four of these binary radio periods correspond to previously known neutron star X-ray binaries, while two of the newly discovered binary radio periods are associated with the known millisecond pulsars, E03 and E17. Additionally, the findings include three new millisecond pulsars discovered within globular clusters: ATCA J172459.5-3605.3, ATCA J173840.4-2745.3, and ATCA J174435.5-2739.8, along with two new neutron star X-ray binaries discovered within globular clusters: ATCA J172459.5-3605.3, linked to the X-ray source CX4, and ATCA J173840.4-2745.3, linked to the X-ray source CX5. The directionality of emission from lasers can be characterized by a divergence angle, which indicates how broadly emitted light spreads. Due to the nature of transverse modes in standard single-transverse-mode lasers, their emission directionality is largely consistent, with a divergence angle ranging approximately 1 degree to 30 degrees. In contrast, resonator designs based on circle dividers can produce unpredictable light emission patterns, which may not reflect the actual mode properties. This phenomenon is illustrated using a 532 nm Nd:YAG laser equipped with an external cavity and a circle divider mirror. When testing the beam quality, we observed a marked increase in the divergence angle from approximately 1.3 degrees to as wide as 40 degrees, despite the laser operating in a single-transverse-mode state. This abnormal emission pattern was investigated in relation to the circle divider mirror and its effect on the laser's operation. It was found that certain adjustments to the circle divider angle could significantly reduce the divergence angle to as low as 0.57 degrees, thereby improving the beam quality (BQ) factor to 1060, which represents an improvement of 206 from the baseline BQ factor of -109. This notable improvement in the BQ factor was achieved by adjusting the circle divider angle to split the propagating mode into two components, with the larger component contributing to the forward propagation and the smaller component contributing to the lateral emission. It was observed that the beam quality could be optimized through adjustment of the circle divider angle, with the desired emission pattern resulting from a combination of the original mode and a higher-order mode. It was also found that the optimized beam could be obtained over a range of up to 10 W of output power. Moreover, the directionality of emission was found to be highly sensitive to changes in the circle divider angle, particularly when the angle deviated significantly from the optimized value. It was further noted that the circle divider design plays a crucial role in determining the directionality of emission, and that a well-designed circle divider can effectively split the propagating mode to achieve the desired emission pattern. Offline learning for multi-agent systems typically involves training individual agents without any interaction, which can result in poor performance due to the lack of shared experience among agents. To address this issue, we introduce the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework, which introduces a novel way to represent shared experiences through individual trajectories. In this framework, shared knowledge is captured by encoding inter-trajectory similarities and intra-trajectory differences. It is shown that the diversity of trajectories contributes to the learning process and offline data utility. The SIT framework is applied to an offline multi-agent reinforcement learning setting, and an effective algorithm is proposed to extract shared knowledge and individual trajectories. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate the benefits of the SIT framework in promoting diverse offline data exploration and efficient offline learning. The proposed methods demonstrate superior performance compared to current multi-agent offline learning algorithms. In addition, an analysis of the diversity of individual trajectories and their contribution to offline data utility is provided through metric-based evaluations. The SIT framework is also applicable to real-world scenarios involving multi-agent interactions, as demonstrated in our offline data examples derived from the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset. The code is available at: \url{https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/NMJRL}. Our research reveals that in these systems, entanglement within individual spins can generate nonlocal effects and steer quantum states, although the actual impact relies heavily on the specific layout of the system's architecture. We further establish that varying the parameters of the Heisenberg interaction can alter the distribution of single-particle entanglement, thereby nonlocal effects and the ability to control quantum states. Notably, our study shows that in these systems, single-particle entanglement can exhibit distinct patterns of growth at alternating momentum values. We propose that these observations could provide the basis for experimenting with single-particle entanglement in Heisenberg spin chains using pulses of laser light. Our findings also suggest that entanglement within individual spins can contribute significantly to nonlocal effects and the ability to control quantum states in multi-partite systems. Nonetheless, our results indicate that in these systems, single-particle entanglement is not the predominant factor governing nonlocal phenomena and the ability to control quantum states, particularly at high momentum values. We predict that our findings could be applied to a broader range of systems characterized by similar Heisenberg interactions. Moreover, we anticipate that our study will contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between single-particle entanglement and nonlocal effects in quantum systems, encompassing Heisenberg spin chains and systems described by the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger Hamiltonian. The 2018 eruption of the nova V392 Persei provided a rare opportunity to monitor a binary nova system in real-time. By analyzing V392 Persei during its initial phase, researchers discovered a substantial increase in gamma-ray bursts at an energy level of 10 MeV, suggesting a significant enhancement in the nucleon flux resulting from the nova's explosion. According to theoretical models, the nova's outer layer inhibits the flow of high-energy particles from the binary system's neutron stars or black hole, implying that a massive increase in these particles could indicate a significant alteration in the nova's accretion state. Additionally, V392 Persei's gamma-ray spectrum exhibited a notable hard component, featuring a significant energy spectrum of 10 MeV and was also characterized by marginal polarization and an irregular pulse period. These characteristics suggest that the gamma-ray emission observed from V392 Persei during its initial phase are a product of ultra-high energy particles originating from a relativistic population of nucleon particles, likely generated by the interaction between the nova's explosion and the binary system's magnetic field. Furthermore, measurements indicate that the relativistic nucleon particles had a pulse period of roughly one day and could be observed from the Earth for approximately 150 days following the nova's explosion. Consequently, the Earth is likely to experience additional gamma-ray bursts from this binary system, specifically targeting high-energy particles and providing a chance to study the binary system's accretion state, including any potential changes, through the analysis of gamma-ray bursts encountered during the anticipated recurrent nova eruption in 2023. The V392 Persei Nova Monitoring Project has been established to carry out this analysis by continuously observing the system via gamma-ray monitors and by conducting in-depth investigations of anticipated gamma-ray bursts. The success of this project relies heavily on the participation of the community in the data analysis process. Therefore, the project invites researchers to contribute their expertise and participate in the analysis of the collected data in order to gain a deeper understanding of the binary nova system V392 Persei and the underlying physics governing its behavior. The project also provides researchers with a chance to monitor a binary nova system that is anticipated to erupt again in the near future, offering a chance to study a rare phenomenon. The project's website, which includes the particle data archive, is accessible at https://v392persei.space.gov. By joining this project, researchers can contribute to the analysis of the binary nova system V392 Persei and the Earth's gamma-ray burst data, in addition to advancing their own research goals. To assess the accuracy of quantum gates on real-world hardware, we suggest using a pair of entangled states based on the toric code, which are highly robust to noise. A small set of measurement outcomes, specifically the "check" measurements associated with the toric code, provides sufficient information to evaluate the fidelity of the entangled state and associated single-qubit operations. We demonstrate that this protocol is resilient to faulty quantum circuits and noisy measurements, yielding an unambiguous pass/fail indicator for each check measurement, even if individual qubits behave erratically. Furthermore, we incorporate Bayesian statistics to estimate the fidelity of quantum operations despite measurement errors, using a conservative approach to ensure broad applicability. We illustrate the potential of this approach with numerical simulations involving realistic models of quantum hardware. Additionally, we outline strategies to optimize the entangled state preparation process and reduce the number of qubits required for the test. Finally, we discuss potential experiments based on current quantum experimentation platforms.

We investigate current properties on the surface of a two-dimensional, weakly coupled superfluid or superconducting phase, specifically focusing on an anisotropic lattice. A precise diagrammatic approach allows us to develop a robust expression for surface local currents in both bosonic and fermionic scenarios. Our analysis reveals that surface currents display persistent and directionally dependent characteristics, aligned with underlying lattice directions, and comprising two distinct components: a coherent phase current and a dissimilar edge current. The phase current is dictated by the mass term and is anisotropically persistent in motion, while the edge current is directed towards slowing down the edge motion. Both the phase and edge currents contribute to a dissipation effect on their own motion, albeit through different mechanisms. We explore the relationship between these surface currents and edge modes found in the lattice version of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula. In both bosonic and fermionic cases, we find that the edge current coefficient correlates with the coefficient of the linear disorder term in the electrical conductivity equation from the 5-dimensional Feynman-Hellman method. Furthermore, we find that the phase current plays a role in the lattice version of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula, and both current components are relevant in the context of quantum transport in lattice systems. We also examine the implications of our findings for the entropy generation process and discuss possible connections to research on the Wieder crystal model and the Harper model. Our study provides a novel insight into the properties of surface currents in weakly coupled superfluid or superconducting phases and offers a new perspective on edge modes in these systems. The proposed diagrammatic approach can be further expanded to study other current-related phenomena in these systems. Understanding how knowledge evolves over time is crucial for navigating the vast amount of existing knowledge. In recent years, High-Energy Physics (HEP) experiments have generated immense amounts of data, leading to a significant expansion of high-energy physics knowledge. To effectively manage this knowledge, it's essential to monitor the quantifiable index of knowledge (KQI) as it relates to research findings. In this paper, we develop a method to measure the knowledge evolution of four prominent arXiv categories in hEP and analyze how it correlates with publication activity in those areas. Our approach combines natural language processing and machine learning techniques to categorize publication content according to six knowledge categories, allowing us to track the knowledge progression over time. The extensive, persistent polar vortices in a planet's stratosphere are areas where the atmosphere rotates at a different pace, isolated from the faster rotation rates nearby. These vortices form due to a combination of a planet's rotational characteristics and the shape of its polar region, which affects the movement of air there. On the planet Jupiter, a constant North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV) has been observed for many years, and it shares similarities with the polar vortices found on the planet Earth. In comparison to the NPSV on Jupiter, the SSPV is less stable and exists for a shorter period of time. This difference in vortex stability is attributed to the distinct atmospheric conditions found on the two planets, which affect the formation and duration of these polar vortices. Using the Mott-Seitz model, we calculate a square root relationship between the energy barrier for non-radiative decay and the oxidation energy of an excess electron in an anionic cluster. This cluster, consisting of 13 atoms from the group of metals and halogens, is arranged in a cubic structure and has a single extra electron in a d-band. We analyze how the energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital change with increasing oxidation energy, and find that they follow the same trend as predicted by the Mott-Seitz model. This result is validated through more accurate quantum mechanical calculations using the method of density functional theory, where we consider several different types of barriers for decay and find that they can be well-represented by a linear combination of two types of barriers, one of which is the square root relationship predicted by the Mott-Seitz model. We also find that at high oxidation energies, the quantum mechanical calculations can produce results that differ significantly from the Mott-Seitz model, but that these deviations become small at lower oxidation energies. We further find that the density functional theory can produce two types of profiles for decay, one of which corresponds to the square root relationship predicted by the Mott-Seitz model, and that this type of profile is more stable than the other type. We conclude that the Mott-Seitz model can provide a good estimate of the decay profile when the excess electron is localized in a high density region, but that more accurate quantum mechanical calculations are needed to determine the total energy and the stable state of the excess electron when the excess electron is delocalized over a large area. We also suggest that the Mott-Seitz model can be used to estimate the energy barrier for decay in other systems that involve an excess electron in a d-band. We finally discuss some possibilities for improving the Mott-Seitz model by incorporating more accurate predictions of molecular orbital energies. Inspired by the fundamentals of neural networks, specifically their analogy to the brain's functioning, we present an alternative training method called error backmapping. In traditional neural network training, errors are propagated backwards to adjust weights and biases, whereas in error backmapping, errors are determined by calculating the difference between actual and predicted outputs at each neural network layer. Our research utilizes a simple neural network to demonstrate the viability of error backmapping, resulting in a more transparent and predictable training process. However, further experimentation reveals that error backmapping trains neural networks more slowly than the standard method. Consequently, our analysis indicates that errors backmap in the opposite direction than previously assumed and that the alleged 'feedback' nature of neural networks is actually a misconception. Despite this, neural networks can still learn effectively using the standard training method. In conclusion, while our proposed training algorithm demonstrates theoretical merit, it appears that neural networks learn more efficiently through the standard training method. Therefore, there is no practical advantage to using error backmapping. Nevertheless, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the neural network training process. We have developed a collective theory for magnetic skyrmions that applies to
any lattice structure and represents the population of these topological objects
as a continuous field varying across homotopy groups. Our approach is based on
a coarse-graining procedure that takes into account the local skyrmion density and
their spatial orientation, mapped to a higher-dimensional space using the
Sine-Gordon model framework. This method preserves the original interactions among
skyrmions and facilitates a dynamic description. We studied the phenomena at
which skyrmions approach and interact with domain walls within a cube lattice
structure and discovered that our model yields a similar 2D monodromy diagram for
the skyrmion-domain wall interactions, despite differences in lattice
structures... This leads to scenarios where domain walls can pin multiple skyrmion
types, all of which can independently move while intersecting only at the point
of pinning. Furthermore, our theory can be expanded to include interactions with
other topological objects and predicts the existence of a previously unreported
skyrmion type that can exist within lattices structured as a pentagonal grid. 
We also derive a simplified 'X-theorem' which can be applied to describe
interaction effects in lattices that are close to square or triangular in
structure. This study provides a foundation for a new perspective on the study
of magnetic skyrmions, where they are viewed as part of a continuous field that
can be manipulated to achieve desired outcomes. This approach has the potential
to tackle intricate problems associated with the behavior of these objects at
higher population levels.  Our research is now available as a full paper on
arXiv.

We examine how the electron-electron Coulomb interaction affects the convergence of self-consistent Hartree-Fock solutions within a finite basis set context. Our analysis indicates that, unlike the Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov approach, the Hartree-Fock method does not exhibit divergent behavior due to two-body correlations. Nonetheless, increasing the basis set does not yield significant improvements in Hartree-Fock calculations for systems with strong electron-electron interactions. This limitation stems from the inadequacy of single-determinant wavefunctions in capturing two-body correlations essential to understanding antiferromagnetic interactions. To overcome this, we propose combining Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov calculations with large basis sets to obtain two-body correlation functions, thereby obtaining insight into the antiferromagnetic interactions without having to resort to complicated four-body calculations. As an example, we apply this approach to Cu$^{2+}$ ions in the antiferromagnetic Mott insulator La$_2$CuO$_4$.

In explosive synchronization transitions, a sudden shift from disordered movement to coordinated rhythm occurs, commonly seen in heart rate and breathing patterns. This phenomenon is highly influential, with researchers actively debating its underlying causes and implications for complex systems. Studies have shown that the structure of networks plays a crucial role in exploiting the benefits of explosive transitions, allowing for significant gains in efficiency and effectiveness. However, a key question remains unanswered: do explosive transitions offer a competitive advantage only when the dynamics of networks is highly structured, or can it be beneficial in scenarios with high levels of dynamical disorder. To address this question, researchers analyzed the behavior of networks subject to random fluctuations and oscillations, and found that explosive transitions can occur even in networks with high dynamical disorder, providing a major advantage when structure and dynamics are both optimized. Furthermore, they found that the benefit of explosive transitions can be derived from the network's architecture, and demonstrated this through a theoretical model that reproduces the observed effects. Interestingly, this model indicates that explosive transitions can be obtained through different mechanisms, including the formation of hierarchical clusters, and suggests that this could be the case in biological systems that exhibit rapid switching between ordered and disordered states, such as the brain during sleep. Overall, this study provides a new perspective on the explosive transition phenomenon, and highlights its competitive benefit as a coordinate switch that can be achieved through various means, offering a more versatile and multifaceted understanding of this complex phenomenon. This work is particularly significant, as it sets the stage for the exploration of more advanced dynamics in network systems that interact with their environment, and raises thought-provoking questions about the nature of explosive transitions in such systems. Ultimately, this study invites researchers to reevaluate their perspective on complex systems, and consider the possibility that explosive transitions may be the rule, rather than the exception. This result is further utilized to develop a fast and flexible inexact successful geodesic method (ISGM) for solving the matrix optimization problem, where the subproblem solves can be non-monotone, leading to an inexact solution. The method involves two parameter settings: one setting where the inexact solution to the subproblem can be non-monotone, and another where the inexact solution must be non-monotone. Both settings guarantee the convergence to a critical point, while the choice of parameters can guarantee the strong convexity and smoothness of the geodesic trajectory. Notably, when the subproblem solver is exact, the method reduces to the original successful geodesic method (SGM), which guarantees the strong convexity and smoothness of the geodesic trajectory. To further improve the method, an inexact two-loop variant of ISGM is developed, where an approximate solution to the subproblem can be used to update the parameter in the inner loop, leading to an inexact solution to the subproblem in the outer loop. The inexact two-loop variant of ISGM guarantees the strongest convexity and smoothness of the geodesic trajectory. The method ISGM has the best known worst-case O(1/T^2) rate of convergence, and the method INETLSGM has the best known worst-case O(1/T) rate of convergence. The method INETLSGM is compared to the state-of-the-art methods LSSGM and FBS, where INETLSGM achieves the fastest known average convergence rate. A study is presented to examine the background of gravitational waves resulting from the decay of heavy elements in the early universe's quadratic phase. Our research focuses on scalar fields with the same spin and multiplicity, and we develop their decay product background's spectrum. Furthermore, we investigate the overlap between this background and primordial black hole formation, and found that future gravitational wave detectors could distinguish between the two by observing the background's power spectrum at different scales. If the universe's quadratic phase contains multiple heavy elements decaying at varying times, the background's power spectrum may be more complex, and we present a general framework for this scenario. Meanwhile, the background may also be affected by the universe's quadratic phase's vacuum structure, specifically the formation of condensates, and we found that their decay could produce a background with distinct features. Our research investigates how helical swimmers navigate through a viscous fluid under the influence of forces like gravity, which affects their motion. We study and analyze different snowman-like configurations, which exhibit a peculiar balance of forces. In this case, we find that the most stable structure, where the head and tail weigh the same, is not the optimal choice for movement. Instead, a balance where one section is slightly heavier than the other is more beneficial for movement. This section will then move through the fluid with a loopy pattern, eventually causing the whole swimmer to shift and reset its balance, only to repeat the cycle. This behavior is seen at all scales, from micro helical swimmers to large snowman-like structures, and even affects how surface swimmers move when influenced by gravity. This effect leads to the swimmer's speed increasing with the strength of these forces, up to a point, where it begins to impede movement. This pattern of movement can be understood through a simplified model that focuses on the interaction between the swimmer and the fluid. This research provides valuable insights into the motion of helical swimmers and offers opportunities to explore this topic through hands-on experiments. This work is a preliminary step toward understanding how helical swimmers can adapt to different environments and navigate complex pathways. This work has been finalized and is ready for publication. This could involve exploring how surface swimmers are influenced by gravity at a more in-depth level, or studying how forces like gravity and surface tension combine to affect the snowman-like effect. This effect could also be investigated in relation to other forces that may shape the balance of helical swimmers, such as electrical forces, which could lead to the discovery of new, optimized configurations. This research provides a foundation for a broader investigation into the motion of helical swimmers and the role that balance plays in this process. This study explores how the Hamming distance from optimal solutions evolves during
optimization processes driven by co-evolutionary genetic algorithms, comparing social
learning to individual learning strategies. Our analysis focuses on the Hamming distance
expected value at equilibrium points resulting from these learning strategies. Our data
shows that, regardless of the learning approach used, the Hamming distance from optimal
solutions initially decreases over time. However, it becomes clear that, as the optimization
process reaches its equilibrium, the Hamming distance expects value differs between social
and individual learning scenarios. Interestingly, the structure of Hamming distance trajectories
under social and individual learning can be distinguished. To further investigate this
finding, a theoretical model was developed and used to compare the Hamming distance values
from social and individual learning in equilibrium. Our results indicate that, as the
population size increases, the Hamming distance value from social learning approaches the
value from individual learning, thus validating our data analysis. Additionally, our
results highlight that population sizes as low as 4-8 can already lead to Hamming distance
values from social learning comparable to individual learning values. To rule out
biases from our specific GA implementation, our results were validated using the L Shark
algorithm. Our conclusions highlight the superior performance of social learning over individual
learning, suggesting that social learning yields optimized solutions at a faster rate. 
This leads to the recommendation to consider social learning algorithms for problems where
Hamming distance optimization is key. Moreover, our findings provide valuable insights into
the mechanisms driving optimization processes in co-evolutionary genetic algorithms. 
This research offers an analytical perspective on the application of co-evolutionary 
genetic algorithms in optimization processes and suggests possible future directions 
for related research. This study's data and theoretical model findings can be used as a 
benchmark for comparisons with other co-evolutionary learning strategies. 
This research data is supported by 10 plots and 5 tables highlighting key results, 
along with 100 data points for each of the 4 considered population sizes.

We investigated the role of aerosolized droplets in the spread of COVID-19 by analyzing factors that influence their behavior under gravity in air. A detailed mathematical model describes the motion of these droplets, which we apply to different scenarios, including exhaled breath and falling droplets entering a body of water. To further understand the spread of the infection, we used numerical simulations to examine how droplet size, shape, and weight impact COVID-19 transmission, in addition to other environmental factors that affect the infection risk. Our simulations suggest that to significantly reduce the spread of COVID-19, it is essential to implement measures that minimize the release of aerosolized droplets, particularly those in the larger size range. This could be achieved by enhancing air ventilation, enforcing social distancing rules, and using face masks that filter out contaminated droplets. Our study's findings can contribute to the development of more effective strategies to contain the spread of COVID-19. Furthermore, the mathematical model we introduced can be adapted to study the behavior of aerosolized droplets carrying other pathogens. It is also possible to modify the model to explore the impact of COVID-19 aerosol transmission dynamics in various enclosed environments. For instance, we could incorporate mobility patterns of individuals into the model to analyze the effects on infection transmission and distribution within buildings. This extends the conventional compartmental model, also known as the susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) model, by considering the effects of aerosolized droplets on the spread of the infection. Livingston, as well as the initial model developed by Ross, Ross, and Tom. In contrast, our model builds upon their work to address this gap. Inverse and ill-posed problems have been a persistent obstacle in various disciplines and have been addressed with some success using regularization methods and statistical interpretations. Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly the success of very deep neural networks in solving inverse problems can be attributed to their ability to learn end-to-end solutions, eliminating the need for traditional techniques of solving forward problems or inverting signals. This paper delves into the relationship between neural networks and inverse problems, examining how they leverage network properties to bypass conventional ill-posedness remedies. It further explores ways to combine neural networks with statistical interpretations and discusses potential challenges related to their scalability and stability. Examples of inverse problems such as compressive sensing, image deblurring, MRI reconstruction, and face reconstruction from limited data are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of neural networks in solving these problems. Finally, this paper discusses future research directions and associated open questions in this field. edge ideals, resulting in the derivation of equalities and inequalities for the
ordinary and symbolic power of edge ideals. Additionally, new formulas are
obtained for the equalizing power in complex scenarios and interesting patterns
are identified in their structural composition. These results present a thorough
exploration of the equality of ordinary and symbolic power of edge ideals,
offering a comprehensive framework for this phenomenon and revealing the
underlying structural features responsible for it.

Building upon previous work, we examine the generalization of the Jordanian twist and its relationship to the simple Jordanian twist under Lie algebra deformation. We demonstrate that the generalized Jordanian twist can be successfully achieved through a simple twist of the algebra $so(4)$, thereby establishing a connection between the two. Furthermore, we derive the explicit form of the generalized Jordanian twist and confirm that it adheres to the principle of being analytically soluble. Additionally, we establish the precise form of its solvable structure and discuss the related issues of generalization and the principle of simplicity. Lastly, we explore the potential for analogous connections to the Heisenberg twist and the harmonic twist.

Similar to other complex systems, the spread of civil unrest in urban settings is driven by interconnected events with varying intensities, occurring against a complex urban backdrop that includes interlinked infrastructure, and is shaped by historical developments and social dynamics. Despite the recognized significance of this phenomenon, there is a recognized gap in modeling the interplay between the structural foundations of a city, its infrastructure, and the occurring events of unrest. To address this, we introduce a new kind of multi-scale network model that incorporates the coexistence of densely connected unrest networks and the more fragmented geographical structure of the city. These opposing characteristics are showcased through empirical analysis of an Italian city, and the suggested model is put to the test using empirical unrest data, and is shown to be favoured over a random model following the application of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Furthermore, our model reveals that the distribution of event intensities can be described by a Levy distribution, and is influenced by the presence of highly connected unrest hubs. These findings are further validated through the simulation of an epidemic model that is capable of jumping between different levels of the city's structure. Our research provides a method for analyzing the interplay between event intensity and network topology in urban unrest scenarios, and can serve as a foundation for the study of other urban phenomena influenced by complex networks. The available data for unrest events allows for the empirical analysis of our model, and it is available for further research alongside the implemented simulation code. The multi-scale nature of this model offers a novel perspective on the study of urban networks, and it is feasible that the described architecture shares similarities with other complex network systems that are yet to be understood. The empirical unrest data used in this research is part of the University of Oxford Civil Unrest Dataset, and is hosted by the Penn State University's Institute for Computational Social Science. The dataset is also freely accessible through the package's reference link. The presented model is implemented in Python 3, and the code is available for replication purposes alongside the underlying unrest data, and can be found at the listed repository. The described architecture of this network model offers several key features that are relevant to the analysis of urban unrest, and are capable of facilitating the transfer of information between differently connected networks. It is conceivable that similar multi-scale network architectures exist in other complex network systems that are yet to be understood. We introduce a novel perspective on the knowledge amalgamation problem, which involves a student model learning from multiple instructor models. A saliency-based method is proposed to identify the most effective combinations of instructor models, by analyzing the model components that contribute to accurate student output. This approach, compared to a random amalgamation strategy, leads to a 78% reduction in average regret over a diverse set of datasets. Furthermore, the saliency-based method is shown to achieve optimal subgame equilibrium in a multi-instructor scenario, and is demonstrated through an illustrative example. The method is computationally efficient, enabling its application to large-scale deep neural networks. The benefits of this approach are realized through an ensemble of the student model with the amalgamated instructor models, resulting in a 9% improvement in test accuracy. The framework is overarching, applicable to any model that can be optimized through stochastic gradient descent. The code for the proposed method is publicly available.

Additionally, we found that among the 27 S4 quartic extensions with a rational rank of 0, there were 11, 8, 7, and 1 extensions with elliptic curves of rank not greater than 1, not greater than 2, not greater than 3, and not greater than 4, respectively. Our findings indicate that over half of the S4 quartic extensions have a rational rank of 0 or 1, which provides significant implications for the rank of moduli spaces of coverings and a counterweight to the generic case of S4 extensions having higher-ranked elliptic curves. Our work also establishes relationships between the weights of Hilbert modular forms and the ranks of corresponding elliptic curves, and we concretely determined the weights corresponding to some specific forms, which in turn enabled us to draw conclusions about the ranks of certain elliptic curves. A promising route to exceling tensor network methods lies in recognizing that both causal
consistency and localizability are equivalent to allowing tensor networks to be viewed as
quantum circuits dependent on specific parameters. By leveraging the vast experience in
using such circuits for quantum computation, we can create a powerful toolkit to develop
well-performing tensor network algorithms. As evidence, we display several propagation
methods based on quantum circuit representations of tensor networks, outperforming existing
methods in most cases. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the incorporation of
artificial neural networks into tensor networks by providing a method to parameterize the
entanglement structure. We also demonstrate that certain circuit representations can
result in tensor networks with intrinsic time-ordering, allowing for the simulation of
systems involving particle backflow, such as time-local Hamiltonians with particle
backflow. Additionally, we show that certain circuit representations can yield tensor
networks equivalent to the multi-time density matrix matrix renormalization group (MT-SING
trons) algorithm, a powerful algorithm that comprehensively integrates all previous
renormalization group methods by approximating the multi-time density matrix instead
of specific snapshots. We anticipate that our findings will motivate a thorough
exploration of the MT-SING trons algorithm's capabilities in relation to other renormalization
group methods. All our code is openly accessible for replication and further
development at https://github.com/QuDaQuAntum/TensorNetworksAsQuantumCircuits. We look
forward to collaborating with other researchers to unlock the full potential of this
approach. We also include a listing of the parameters used for our examples to aid in
reproduction.

In cancer research, understanding the disease's progression and development is crucial for developing effective treatments. To achieve this, graph neural networks have shown significant promise in analyzing complex tissue structures and their relationships. However, existing approaches require extensive training data and a deep understanding of the disease's biology. In order to streamline the classification of cancer tissue representations and facilitate faster exploration of the parameter space, we introduce the concept of transfer learning. By leveraging pre-trained models that capture general patterns and characteristics, we can refine them for specific tissue types and conditions. We tested this approach on two distinct datasets: one for renal carcinoma and the other for pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Our results demonstrated that graph neural networks can accurately classify tissue representations with minimal training, outperforming baseline models that rely solely on training data. Additionally, we discovered that using pre-trained models enables the classification of similar tissue types and conditions. We further analyzed the influence of distinct protein markers on the disease's progression and development. Our findings provide a solid foundation for employing graph neural networks in cancer research and pave the way for investigating the disease's biology. We made our code and datasets publicly available to facilitate further research and improve the accuracy of classifications.

To accelerate the computation of gravitational interactions in large astrophysical simulations, we integrated the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) into the Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) framework of the EnZone code. This improvement enables us to tackle a critical bottleneck in high-resolution simulations. By converting O(N^2) operations into O(N), FMM reduces the computational time by leveraging a hierarchical method to calculate interactions between particles. We integrated FMM with a particle mesh method and established a code that can handle a range of astrophysical simulations, including gas dynamics and gravitational physics, within an AMR framework. Through a series of tests, we evaluated the performance enhancements brought by FMM and its interaction with other parallelization techniques. FMM led to a significant increase in physical time-step iterations and allowed us to utilize more precise gravitational softening volumes, which is particularly important for star-forming region simulations. Moreover, we observed parallel scalability with both OpenMP and MPI, and our results demonstrated the potential of the code to model the evolution of large galaxies through multiple Hubble timescales. The current version of the code is available for download and further development through its GitHub repository.

This paper introduces a novel contrastive learning algorithm for cross-anatomy domain adaptation, which enables the segmentation of complex anatomical structures in unfamiliar domains using limited labeled data and plentiful unlabeled data. Our method, called Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA), incorporates a contrastive loss function to systematically minimize the differences between similar tissues across domains, thereby expanding the expertise of our model to a new domain. We leverage the availability of unlabeled data in each domain to develop unique adapters for each domain, ensuring that our experts and adapters accurately map similar tissues and adapt this expertise to each domain. Our results demonstrate that CS-CADA achieves superior segmentation performance compared to existing domain adaptation methods, showcasing potential applications in various anatomical domains such as brain, abdomen, and lung. Moreover, CS-CADA enhances expert expertise across different categories of organs of dissimilar shapes and types. Our implementation and data are freely accessible online.

Building upon previous work, this study finds the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation of a massless scalar CFT$_2$ conformal block of a conserved current. The representation is validated by examining its boundary field theory and AdS$_3$ geodesic operator counterpart in the $1/N$ limit. The former reveals a shift in spin from $h$ to $h-1$ for the CFT$_2$ conformal block, while the latter yields an additional spin $h$ term in the $1/N$ limit. Additionally, this study derives the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation for a massless scalar CFT$_2$ conformal block associated with a conserved three-current. The representation is found to be invariant to the spin transformation identified previously. Our team discovered the supernova SN~2020jfo in February 2020, which was initially mistaken for the return of a dormant black hole candidate cygnus X-1. However, spectroscopic analysis during SN~2020jfo's nebular phase revealed that the object is actually a stellar eruption or a supernova originating from a binary companion. SN~2020jfo's spectrum during its early stages indicated a spectral type of Type II, characterized by strong hydrogen lines and numerous metal lines. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited unusual absorption features in its H-alpha and H-beta spectra, suggesting that the hydrogen emission arose from a dense, spherical shell with significant microturbulent velocities. By comparing SN~2020jfo to other supernovae, we found that its nickel to iron production ratios are among the highest on record, at 2 times the solar average, while its oxygen to iron ratios are modest and near solar values. Additionally, SN~2020jfo's explosion energy and heavy element abundance were sufficient to produce numerous helium and heavy elements, including strontium, phosphorus, and sulfur, which were confirmed through optical spectroscopy during the nebular phase. Another possible scenario involves a red Supergiant that underwent a merger with a compact object or white dwarf, resulting in thermal energy conversion to heavy elements and the explosion of the supershape. Researchers have noticed a notable trend in the results of cosmological simulations: the composition of haloes is unaffected by the amplitude of primordial perturbations, but their mass is influenced. Further, the relationship between halo mass and location within a cluster seems distorted. Some theories suggest these findings could be explained by the actions of a dark sector with extremely low mass, influencing halo formation on a cluster-sized scale. In this paper, we examine the possibility of such a dark sector affecting cosmological simulations on the same scale. Specifically, we investigate whether a dark sector with negligible mass and a specified density profile can account for the above mentioned effects. Ultimately, we find that it can indeed do so. However, the parameters required to achieve this result are constrained to a degree that seems unlikely given the sector's extremely low mass. We introduce a Convolutional Neural Network and low-rank factorization hybrid approach for piano transcription, combining semi-supervised Canonical Polyadic Decomposition with adaptive constraint adjustments. This model leverages both the power of neural networks to extract complex features and the efficiency of low-rank factorization in modeling piano patterns. We demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art low-rank factorization techniques and supervised deep learning methods for piano transcription. Additionally, our model achieves high accuracy despite limited labeled data, surpassing the performance of supervised baselines and achieving comparable results to an all-note-labeled baseline while being significantly more efficient in terms of training time. We validate our approach through comprehensive experiments on the MapReduce-based CANARY dataset and present a detailed analysis of our results. The code for our method is openly available at https://github.com/hjdw/hjdw-homepage/tree/main/piano_transcription.

This research introduces an original approach to assigning properties like mass, specific angular momentum, and entropy to individual fluid elements within a rotating star. In contrast to conventional methods, which determine these properties by interpolating between global averages, our approach utilizes a local reference frame that accounts for conservation principles. Although this method appears to lead to diverse property distributions, our analysis reveals that, for steady-state configurations, the usual rotational modulation of surface characteristics is reproduced. Additionally, we find that traditional first-order approximations, such as the baricentric frame, still provide accurate representations of property distributions. To facilitate numerical implementations, our choice includes a set of simple and efficient algorithms for calculating essential variables within each fluid element, including mass, specific angular momentum, entropy, and potential temperature. To validate our approach, we perform a series of numerical experiments involving non-axisymmetric rotational mixing in both subgiant and giant stars, and our results demonstrate significant enhancement of elemental abundance patterns in the surfaces of these stars. The proposed framework is now available online as an open-source software.

The success of machine learning models heavily relies on accurate and abundant labeled data. Selective labeling techniques have gained popularity by enabling experts to focus their time on the most crucial examples, leaving less important ones unlabeled. In this work, we introduce a new framework that leverages stochastic optimization and learning dynamics to effectively utilize selective labels. We demonstrate the benefit of this approach by applying it to a common classification task and showing that even with only expert time spent on examples influencing the model's decisions, the algorithm achieves optimal label efficiency. Furthermore, our method surpasses alternative label utilization strategies in scenarios where models learn from repeated selective labeling processes. We also highlight the framework's potential to enhance existing selective labeling methods through an example optimization path. We validate the method's effectiveness with both synthetic data and real-world settings, involving the reduction of misclassified selective labels in an email spam classification dataset. Code is available at: https://github.com/google-research-datahq/SelectiveLabelingOptimization.

Our analysis of online forums representing diverse communities reveals a sudden drop in topic variety in March 2020, which normalized to pre-pandemic levels by the following winter. However, a notable decrease in variety persisted in these communities through 2021, with no full recovery observed. Furthermore, our findings indicate that online social connections are more resistant to change than the underlying community dynamics, with a notable divergence in reaction times. For example, the time taken for the word "vaccine" to become a common online discussion topic differed significantly between the two groups. Our research suggests that the response of online communities to changes reflects a residual effect of the pandemic's initial shock on variety, with no full recovery in the next two years. The associated project 'Citizen Perceptions of the Pandemic' provides an unusual data set spanning 24 months, offering an exceptional opportunity to study the long-term, unforeseen effects of the pandemic on urban encounters and community resilience. The approach uses data from simultaneous measurements of surface tension and buoyancy force at multiple points, applying a modified version of the method developed by its creators in [5]. The existing algorithm only considers cases where the frequency of ripples is greater than that of the primary waves. This improved method can also handle situations where the frequencies are equal. The spread of fake news through social media has become a pressing concern in the fight against disinformation. Machine learning models that learn from the context in which information is presented have shown potential in combating this issue effectively. As these models typically operate on multi-layered datasets consisting of various sections including the article itself, the context of the situation it refers to, and any comments made in response, we believe it's time to revisit traditional evaluation methods. In our study, we examine how context affects the performance of fake news detection models and introduce a novel assessment strategy that differentiates between in-context and out-of-context learning techniques. Our research utilizes the Google Advanced Multimedia Dataset (GAMEDO) consisting of 11,000 samples, to compare conventional evaluation methods with our proposed strategy, and our findings demonstrate that machine learning models excel in context and perform better than standard methods by a significant margin of 11%. Moreover, our results indicate that understanding the context within which information is presented improves the effectiveness of fake news detection models even further. We also examine various context designs including sentence-level, paragraph-level, and comment-level context and evaluate the performance of models in both single-step and multi-step reasoning scenarios. Our research paves the way for further investigation into the capabilities of machine learning models in context and suggests that in-context learning can serve as an appropriate evaluation method for fake news detection models. We have conducted additional experiments that demonstrate the superiority of our proposed models over established baselines and are confident that our study will motivate the development of new evaluation strategies for in-context learning. We explore the concept of relative winning conditions in game theory, specifically positioning-based conditions, which take into account the relative distance between players' pieces and a specific location. We define half-positional conditions as a particular type of positioning-based condition, where only the presence or absence of a particular relative distance matters. We investigate conditions that combine multiple half-positional requirements and consider the scenario where certain distances are irrelevant. Our primary focus is on determining whether certain conditions, specifically those based on specific patterns of distances, can be positional or require further analysis. Our study initially assumes a board represented as a finite set of distinct points, and in an additional section, we discuss the implications of our findings on different types of boards. Our research ultimately demonstrates that while some relatively simple positioning-based conditions can be inferred from half-positional conditions, this is not the case for more complex conditions. Additionally, we find that certain conditions based on specific patterns of distances can be non-positional, and this holds true even when we consider only very basic patterns. This advances our previous knowledge, as it was previously unknown whether a condition that combined multiple half-positional requirements could ever result in a non-half-positional condition. Based on a board structure composed of arbitrarily small distances, we prove that any condition that combines multiple half-positional requirements will always be half-positional. X-ray spectra from the Europlexus project's largest database have been examined for a diverse range of cataclysmic variables, revealing distinct insights. The analysis reveals that the X-ray spectra of non-interacting polars are similar to those of interacting polars and cataclysmic variables, exhibiting a spectral structure characteristic of soft X-ray spectra. In contrast, the spectra of asynchronous polars differ, with spectra showing higher temperatures and energy spectra. The temperature variation in soft and hard X-ray spectra exists in most asynchronous polars, with some showing hard X-ray spectral components. These findings suggest that magnetic field interactions cause the variation in X-ray spectra among asynchronous polars, with magnetic reconnection possibly explaining the hard X-ray components. The analysis also enables the development of empirical rules to identify the nature of cataclysmic variables using X-ray spectra. For example, if the temperature of the hard X-ray component is greater than 20 kiloelectronvolts, the system is likely an asynchronous polar. If the hard X-ray component has a similar temperature to the soft X-ray component and if the amplitude of the hard X-ray component is greater than 50%, the system is likely an interactor. These predictions correlate with optical and radio observations, making them useful tools for identifying the nature of cataclysmic variables through X-ray spectra. The analysis also highlights the capability of spectroscopic methods to analyze the geometry of cataclysmic variables. The study's findings are further supported by global response maps, revealing the distribution of the covariance between the parameters of X-ray spectra and the physical properties of the systems. The analysis's results can be utilized to plan observations with instruments like the Europlexus project's Eurosoft, as well as future X-ray missions like ASTROSAT's ASTROSAT-Calvin. The analysis's methodology is applicable to other X-ray spectra analysis of cataclysmic variables and other similar astrophysical objects. The study's results are available in the form of global response maps, providing new insights into the X-ray spectra of a diverse range of cataclysmic variables. In fluid-structure interaction (FSI) applications, a common strategy is to split the simulation framework into two parts: a fluid dynamics module and a solid mechanics module. Typically, the fluid module uses the Navier-Stokes equations, while the solid module uses Hermite type elements to model the structure's behavior. A key challenge in this approach is developing a suitable interface method that efficiently bridges the fluid and solid domains without introducing significant numerical disruption to the simulation. In this paper, we examine various interface methods, focusing on those suitable for partitioned FE-FE approaches, where the fluid and solid problems are solved independently using the finite element method. We review and analyze several methods, including the ALE-based methods, pressure-based methods, counter-flow based methods, and others, discussing their underlying principles, implementation details, and choice of parameters. We also discuss the pros and cons of each method, drawing on recent studies and our own numerical experiments. We offer guidance for researchers and practitioners on selecting the most appropriate interface method for specific FSI applications, given factors such as accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency. We demonstrate the reliability of our recommendations through a range of CFD and FSI simulations, including pulse propagation in a blood vessel, pulmonary airflow, and fluid-structure interaction with an embedded structure. The results show that the most suitable method can significantly affect the accuracy and stability of the simulation, while also influencing the choice of time step and overall computational performance. Through our analysis and numerical experiments, we identify methods that provide high accuracy and stability with efficient time stepping, while also considering the feasibility of implementation. We provide recommendations for selecting the best interface method to achieve the desired balance between accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency in FSI simulations. We also offer our numerical results and associated code for replication of the reported findings. In conclusion, this study offers a comprehensive review of interface methods for FSI simulations, accompanied by practical recommendations and reproducible numerical experiments. It also facilitates further research on this topic by making available customized interface method solvers, along with the code and data for the presented results. Local metric maps in robotics, such as Seemaps, rely on range data and do not account for the structure beyond immediate reach. In contrast, our approach, HiTMap, represents an elevated view of the environment on a higher dimensional surface. By assuming a flat surface, we can use circular regions to organize navigation information, reducing overlap and convergence issues found in tree-based data structures. The HiTMap system consists of three key components: mapping, evaluation, and convergence. It uses an elevated metric map, incorporates navigation feedback in the form of detected obstacles, updates the map accordingly, evaluates the effectiveness of these updates in the form of navigation costs, and converges to the most efficient path by minimizing navigation costs across the map. We demonstrate the capabilities of the HiTMap system through both simulation and actual world tests, showing that it can effectively manage local map updates for efficient navigation by converging to the best path even with moving obstacles. Unlike existing methods, this approach takes into account the diverse paths that light can take, rather than simply determining the characteristics of individual particles. As a result, it provides more accurate results, especially when compared to more complex simulations, and has the added benefit of being more compatible with existing rendering techniques. To evaluate this approach, we apply it to a variety of scenarios, including the simulation of subsurface scattering, metabolic light transportation, and the behavior of light within composite materials, and compare its results to more detailed simulations using a variety of rendering techniques. Our findings indicate that this method produces more accurate results than traditional local approaches and can also be used to enhance the appearance of complex materials. As a result, we believe this approach has the potential to be a more efficient and effective way to simulate the behavior of light within semi-transparent materials. To support this approach, we also introduce a new technique for computing approximate frequencies for use in solving the radiative transfer equation, and provide a software implementation of this method as part of our public repository. As we explore this approach, we also identify several potential areas for further improvement and innovation. As we continue to develop and refine this approach, we invite feedback and contributions from the broader research community. This work provides an original implementation of the calculus of constructions in dependently typed programming languages. Initially developed in the 1980s by Girard, Seldin, and Curry, the calculus of constructions has significantly impacted the development of modern programming languages and type theory. However, a fully functional implementation of the dependent function type in a programming language based on the calculus of constructions has yet to be accomplished. To address this gap, we present CoC2HL, an algorithm that converts programs written in the calculus of constructions into Haskell code. The implementation of this algorithm serves as a basis for an interactive tool accessible via the CoC2HL Web interface. The interface enables users to enter calculus of constructions expressions and automatically generates the corresponding Haskell code. Furthermore, the interface performs static type checking of the generated Haskell code and displays any resulting type errors. As an added feature, the interface includes a link to the Haskell code on the Haskell REPL platform Haskel Cafe. Notably, this implementation achieves a significant advancement over Girard's original algorithm for mirroring terms, and it demonstrates the effectiveness of algorithmic techniques in complex theoretical frameworks. Quantum electronics incorporates the principles of quantum mechanics into the study of electronic devices, offering a detailed understanding of circuit behavior when the size of individual components approaches the nanoscale. Despite the importance of quantum electronics, its fundamental concepts, including entanglement, have not been thoroughly understood, especially in the case of open systems that lack a well-defined steady state. To address this knowledge gap, researchers have developed several methods to quantify entanglement, including the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix approach, which can be applied to system-reservoir combinations to effectively measure entanglement between the system and its environment. Using these methods, along with the Lanczos algorithm, researchers have developed a powerful tool to analyze the dynamics of quantum electronics in relation to the entanglement between the system and its surrounding environment. This approach has been successfully demonstrated through the simulation of a quantum coil field driver. Results showing how entanglement varies with time, as well as its relationship to the characteristics of the reservoir and the system, have been obtained. Furthermore, by modifying the reservoir conditions, researchers were able to transition between different types of entanglement, including partial and cat-state entanglement, or eliminate entanglement entirely. Consequently, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of entanglement in quantum electronics and offers a practical approach to developing technology based on quantum mechanics. To facilitate replication of these findings, detailed parameters for the simulated coil driver, including the parameters used to achieve entangled states, have been included. Replication of these results, along with the calibration of the used methods, is also facilitated through the accompanying code, which is available online. Ultimately, this approach can be applied to any quantum system by modifying the system parameters and the reservoir conditions. In a context where multiple datasets share a common parameter structure, researchers often position a Dirichlet process prior on the density parameters of a single dataset. This typically results in a mixture model with weighted admixture components, with the weights representing the posterior probabilities of the components. However, without additional constraints, the weights become non-identifiable, and the model's parameter space becomes non-estimable. This paper examines how placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities affects the retrieval of identifiable admixture weights and discusses alternative specification of the weights. Additionally, the paper derives closed-form expressions for the posterior weights and discusses their properties in the absence of density constraints. The proposed method can be applied to any Dirichlet process mixture model, and we provide a Python implementation of the algorithms discussed in the paper. We also present an artificial example and a real-world application involving the analysis of functional near-infrared spectroscopy signals, showing the benefits of using the posterior weights. The paper further explores the connection between the posterior weights and Gaussian process objectors, and discusses potential uses in the absence of density constraints. A comprehensive analysis of the two-loop corrections to the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators in QCD has been conducted using the AdS/CFT correspondence. This study evaluated the impact of two-loop effects on the operator mixing and spectrum of low-energy nuclear processes, such as deep inelastic scattering, from a theoretical AdS/CFT perspective. As a result, significant discrepancies up to 30% in the two-loop anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators were found, contradicting previous findings based on the HV rule. Furthermore, this study determined the two-loop mixing coefficients and spectral functions, thereby providing a more accurate understanding of the twist-four operator spectrum. The introduced coefficient ratios can be used as effective observables to investigate the nature of the AdS/CFT correspondence and QCD's underlying dynamics. Additionally, the influence of two-loop effects on the operator spectrum was examined in various AdS/CFT constructions and found to be consistent with previous findings for one-loop effects. However, two-loop corrections significantly altered the operator spectrum, causing shifts of up to 30%, and highlighting the necessity of two-loop accuracy for a precise understanding of the twist-four operator spectrum. The developed framework for two-loop accuracy can be applied to other AdS/CFT constructions and is anticipated to facilitate the computation of higher-loop effects. Nonetheless, the ad hoc inclusion of two-loop effects is deemed insufficient, as it fails to address the fundamental issue of operator mixing beyond the two-loop level. As a result, further research is necessary to resolve the operator mixing issue fully. To address scalability challenges for GPU memory allocation, DynaSOAr was designed as a dynamic system that allocates and manages GPU memory via an address space. By introducing an explicit memory hierarchy and optimizing memory allocation based on application requirements, DynaSOAr enhances memory performance and efficiency. In a benchmark test involving FP32 matrix multiplication, FP64 matrix multiplication, and tree reduction, DynaSOAr demonstrated improved memory utilization and throughput over the traditional $sudo$ allocator and the CUDA dynamic memory allocation function. Additionally, DynaSOAr supported more complex memory configurations and workloads with dynamic memory reordering, whereas the alternative methods struggled or resulted in significant performance degradation. Despite its advancements, DynaSOAr still relies on traditional CUDA kernels and may exhibit memory performance limitations due to GPU hardware constraints. Nevertheless, further innovations in GPU memory allocation, inspired by DynaSOAr's hierarchical approach, have the potential to unlock greater performance potential for future GPU architectures. Our comprehensive theory examines the influence of spin-orbit coupling on YSR state characteristics in proximity to magnetic adatoms or dimers near a silver surface. We demonstrate that for a single adatom, the spin-orbit coupling disrupts the symmetrical distribution of YSR states around the adatom, breaking down the pairing between different orbitals. As a result, the spin-orbit coupling removes the degeneracy of YSR state peaks, causing them to shift in energy. The magnitude of these shifts is highly dependent on the dimensions of the surface Fermi circle and may be insignificant if the YSR state is heavily localized or if there is a significant surface roughness affecting the dimers. However, our model indicates that dimers exhibit unique behavior under the spin-orbit coupling, where the splitting of YSR state peaks can be influenced not only by the adatom parameters but also by the dimensions of the surface and the spin-orbit coupling of the adatom, resulting in possible observations in experiments using magnetic dimers. This study offers a thorough theoretical framework for understanding YSR states in proximity to magnetic adatoms or dimers and has significant implications for the interpretation of experimental results. Furthermore, it highlights the potential for exploring spin-orbit coupling effects in surface systems with adatom or dimer probes.
