This study focuses on the geometry of minimal disks in three-dimensional space, particularly those bounded and entirely within a specific region. We've discovered an instance where the usual symmetry of the disk's geometry breaks down, resulting in an asymmetric configuration. Consequently, this finding indicates that there are multiple distinct types of minimal disks with the same same symmetries as a regular polar disk. Moreover, this implies that certain geodesic rays in the submanifold's metric space are not convergent. The submanifolds whose minimal disks exhibit this behavior include those with polar symmetry and a non-constant curvature function. Notably, this behavior relates to the spectrum of the submanifold, as it includes an infinite number of tunable eigenvalues that can be specified by the values of the disk's radius and growth rate. In the case of surfaces with hyperbolic cusps, the model can be tightened to minimize the eigenvalues, resulting in values that approach zero. However, for a specific range of angles, the model can be tightened to obtain a positive eigenvalue. This positive eigenvalue can be made arbitrarily small, but it cannot be made zero for any polar disk with bounded hyperbolic curvature. Ultimately, this research indicates that submanifolds with complete, bounded minimal disks can have any desired positive or zero eigenvalue, making such submanifolds highly sensitive in the sense of spectral tolerance. This implies that the submanifolds without hyperbolic cusps cannot be locally isometric to the slipping solitons of the Schrodinger equation. A notable arrangement of planets has been identified around the K-dwarf star AD Leo, comprising two mini-Neptunes that transit their star. This discovery was made as a result of the TESS space telescope data, which showed a periodic signal linked to the planets' orbits. Subsequent analysis of the data revealed that the planets reside within the habitable zone of their star, a region typically associated with worlds that support life. Located near the solar system, AD Leo offers a suitable target for study with both the James Webb and a potential near-infrared spectrometer on the Terrestrial Planet Finder. Observations of the star during the TESS mission found it to be rotationally synchronized, which indicates that the stars surface is evenly active and may aid in extracting signature patterns of the planets, ultimately facilitating the determination of their atmospheric composition. Furthermore, AD Leo is set to be one of the largest datasets analyzed by the TESS mission, consisting of nearly daily data for nearly 13 years, which will provide highly accurate measurements of the planets' orbits and a comprehensive understanding of the system. Ultimately, this extensive dataset is expected to pave the way for groundbreaking measurements of the planets' masses and meanings for the field of exoplanetary science. This study introduces the discovered planets, reporting on the analysis of the data and outlining the ongoing efforts to fully characterize the system. It also highlights the significance of AD Leo as a key target for follow-up observations and the opportunities it presents for advancing our understanding of exoplanets through ongoing and future missions.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile TiO2, investigating their behavior both in interstitial and substitutional states. Our analysis, based on first-principles calculations, reveals significant differences in the properties of interstitial and substitutional impurities. In interstitial sites, carbon and nitrogen atoms exhibit similar behavior, with their lone pairs pointing towards neighboring oxygen atoms. This leads to a net attractive interaction with oxygen, resulting in a computed bond length of 0.5 ${\AA}$ and 0.7 ${\AA}$ for C and N respectively, and a corresponding increase in bond energy. In contrast, when these atoms substitute for titanium, the covalent bonds between titanium and oxygen are weakened, leading to a charge transfer from titanium to carbon or nitrogen and a subsequent formation of Ti-O bond alternation. Notably, the energy levels of both interstitial and substitutional impurities lie within the conduction band of TiO2. Our results suggest that both carbon and nitrogen can act as conduction band impurities, with interstitial N having the lowest formation energy of all. This finding is consistent with experimental observations of n-type conductivity in TiO2 after exposure to C or N. Our theoretical predictions are further supported by density of states and formation energy calculations, showing that interstitial C has a relatively high formation energy but can become stable in the presence of oxygen vacancies. These findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding the role of carbon and nitrogen in determining the electrical properties of TiO2. They also offer potential guidance for the development of TiO2-based semiconductor materials with optimized electrical characteristics.

We are studying semi-elastic top-quark decays, specifically looking for variations where the top quark changes its flavor to become a charm or bottom quark. To achieve this, we analyze data from 8 to 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC, using a dataset totaling 139 fb^-1 in size. Our research focuses on analyzing events characterized by an isolated lepton, extra particles in the detector, and missing energy. We've developed an advanced method to calculate the likelihood of observing these events under various conditions, taking into consideration numerous potential variations. By applying these calculations to our data, we've been able to establish upper limits for the branching ratio of the top quark decaying into a charm or bottom quark, missing energy, and extra particles, with values of 0.337 (-0.205) % and 0.188 (-0.115) % at 95% confidence, for respectively elastic and semi-elastic processes, using data from 13 TeV collisions. These results represent the most restrictive upper limits on these processes to date, with our most stringent limit for elastic processes being half the previous best estimate, and for semi-elastic processes being one third of the previous best estimate. Furthermore, we've also established upper limits for the transverse mass of the boson formed from the quark system, missing energy, and extra particles, with values of 684 and 552 GeV at 95% confidence, for respectively elastic and semi-elastic processes, providing the most restrictive limits on these processes as well. Additionally, our research provides a comprehensive analysis of the background for these processes, as well as an evaluation of various irreducible processes that share similar characteristics, with our analysis indicating that a significant anomaly observed in earlier studies, characterized by a multi-TeV resonance, is not supported by our research. Lastly, our study is accompanied by an open data release, enabling further analysis and contributing value to the LHC top-quark physics program.

Researchers Taskay and Kajjalao glared at their proof sheets, wondering why their co-authors had set an impractically low bar for their results. According to the editors, the new bounds they had found were'significantly' better than existing results, yet in the paper, those findings looked... underwhelming. In fact, the new lower limits they had identified were actually worse than the upper limits they had set in some cases. It seemed no one had gotten the memo that in the world of graph theory, the best results were considered the ones that set the upper limits, not the lower ones. With a huff, they decided to revise their paper and include the correct interpretation of their findings. We examined the mass evolution of 205 molecular cores for a period of $\sim 0.4$ million years using a combination of $^{13}$CO and C$^{18}$O data, which are part of the ATLASGAL survey. Our analysis focused on cores within galactic clouds selected based on their mass, density, and velocity dispersion. We compared observed core mass growth to that predicted by a simple gravitational collapse model, finding a significant dispersion in mass evolution. Some molecular cores showed little mass growth, likely due to external influences such as stellar feedback, tidal forces, or internal processes like mass loss from massive protostars. On the other extreme, some cores were rapidly gaining mass, which is difficult to explain without additional physics beyond a simple collapse model. However, we found a significant correlation between mass growth and the presence of formed massive stars, indicating that star formation is a key factor in the mass evolution of molecular cores. This outcome is consistent with observations that show massive star formation often accompanies massive molecular cores. As a result, we anticipate a future correlation between the mass distribution of molecular cores and that of massive stars, which will evolve over millions of years. Furthermore, our data indicate a distinction between single-star and massive-star formation processes, which may result in a massive-star formation threshold influenced by the overall core mass. Finally, our research identifies several cores that have stopped gaining mass and may be contributing to the mass function of low-mass stars, which has yet to be fully understood. Ultimately, monitoring molecular cores over time is essential to comprehending the intricate relationship between them and the formation of massive stars. This knowledge will help answer fundamental questions about how massive-star formation originated in the early universe. We studied the influence of neighboring point context on 3D LiDAR point cloud classification. By examining the effect of context on multiple classification tasks with varying complexity, our findings revealed that context has a positive impact on performance, especially in complex scenarios. Our proposed method, Contextual LiDAR Point Cloud Network (CLPN), successfully incorporates neighboring point context into local context features, leading to improved classification results compared to existing methods. The CLPN approach involves capturing local context features from both individual points and their neighboring points, combining these features and applying them to classification. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed method with various context sizes and multi-scale context, showcasing superior performance in two outdoor scene classification tasks. The evaluation results revealed that the context provided by nearby points is a crucial factor in LiDAR point cloud classification, with contextual information capable of mitigating the limitations of conventional methods in complex scenarios. In particular, our approach achieved outstanding performance on a forest dataset, surpassing the state-of-the-art mean classification accuracy by over 5%. Moreover, we explored the applicability of our method to a road dataset and a dataset with mixted scenes, obtaining comparable performance. Consequently, the context-driven CLPN model is now capable of serving as a baseline for future LiDAR point cloud classification research. The observed ultra-high-energy cosmic ray spectrum appears to correlate with neutrino findings from the AFS and HiRes experiments. Combining these results with recent findings from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and verifying the consistency of the neutrino flux within individual experiments, we notice a noticeable correlation between neutrino and cosmic ray spectra. Moreover, we discovered that the neutrino flux exceeds the cosmic ray spectrum by a factor of roughly three when comparing neutrino and cosmic ray energies. The connection between UHECR and neutrinos suggests that neutrinos represent the secondary particle result of UHECR interactions with interstellar medium, which is consistent with predictions made by (Tinyakov and Charilov, 2013). The long-term stability of liquid foams typically depends on two key factors: the surface tension and the viscosity of the liquid films, as well as the geometric structure of the foam network. However, in certain situations, particularly when dealing with thin films subjected to strong forces, the roughness of these films plays a crucial role in their behavior. Based on principles of continuum mechanics, a model has been developed to describe the flow of liquid films with irregular surfaces, taking into account the effects of surface tension, viscosity, and forced forces. By applying this model to a plate moving through a liquid foam, and using experimental data to inform the simulation, we were able to fit a parameter to the model which correlates with the roughness of the film and varies inversely with the Plateau pressure. This pressure can be seen as a critical stress at which the foam network begins to fail, and it plays a significant role in determining the fate of the films. Furthermore, we found that the film rupture time can be predicted by the model, and the predictions align with existing theories for film behavior under different conditions. While the model requires further development to account for factors like film rupture mechanisms and the effects of forced forces, it provides a useful starting point for understanding and studying the complex behavior of liquid films in foam networks. Upcoming work will see the extension of this model to other types of froths, such as glassy foams composed of non-newtonian liquids. By doing so, it may be possible to clarify the distinctions between forced and steady-state film flows. The model is now available online for download and can be used by researchers to analyze and modify its components. Feedback and suggestions for improvement are also invited. Through this model, we aim to stimulate discussion and contribute to a greater understanding of the intricate dynamics governing liquid films within froth structures. In our research, we aim to combine the capabilities of convolutional neural networks for image classification by utilizing ensemble learning. By creating multiple CNNs with different configuration settings and training them on diverse dataset variations, we develop an ensemble model that outperforms a single, highly optimized CNN. The ensemble comprises seven individual networks, each utilizing unique data augmentations, batch normalization settings, and loss functions, which are then combined through the use of a weighted voting mechanism. The weights are calculated based on the accuracy of each network alone, after which the ensemble model achieves a 0.8% boost in overall accuracy when classifying images in the OuluEye 35 eye region dataset with limited eyes data. Additionally, our method demonstrates superior performance on a larger, more diverse dataset (FaceScrub), resulting in a 11.9% increase in accuracy within the eyes region and a 5.4% improvement for the entire face. Our research demonstrates that ensemble learning can effectively combine the capabilities of CNNs by leveraging diverse network configurations and data processing methods. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/DrMPC/EnsembleConvolutionalNeuralNetworks.

By analyzing two modeling scenarios, we demonstrate that the average work done can be interpreted as the average change in system free energy when it transitions from a microcanonical to a canonical equilibrium state. Additionally, we develop an expression for the work done on a system as it moves from a microcanonical to a granular equilibrium state described by a Gibbs granular free energy expression. We validate our theoretical predictions through numerical simulations of a Lennard-Jones fluid and demonstrate that the work done on the system can be significant, even for systems that appear structurally similar across the microcanonical and canonical descriptions. Moreover, we observe that the work done on the system can be understood in terms of the change in its free energy as it transitions from a microcanonical to a canonical equilibrium state, even when the two structures are distinct. This finding provides a fundamental connection between the concepts of work and free energy in thermodynamics at the micro and macro scales. In recent years, research has expanded on curiosity from a solo-based exploration to a social concept, driven by observations of how individuals are affected by their peers. Recent discoveries suggest that peers can shape curiosity through a process of comparison, where people assess their own levels of interest in relation to those around them. To better understand this phenomenon, our study explores a computational model that incorporates comparison-based curiosity from a self-aware artificial agent to a social network of agents. By applying self-aware architecture to an agent that observes other agents' success levels in problem-solving, our model shows that comparison-based curiosity can emerge through a self-reinforcing loop in a multi-agent system. Moreover, our analysis combines cognitive dynamics with social dynamics to achieve a holistic understanding of how curiosity and social comparison interact, comprising both individual self-aware components and collective effects arising from interacting with others. Finally, our model is applicable to various self-aware multi-agent systems and facilitates the integration of cognitive and social theories. In our experimental setup, our comparison-based curiosity model outperformed alternative approaches by delivering superior results in problem-solving efficiency. Additionally, our analysis of the multi-agent system revealed an interesting effect called "social curvature," which provides further evidence for the validity of our model. In conclusion, our comparison-based curiosity model offers a coherent framework for analyzing complex cognitive and social dynamics and can be adapted to accommodate diverse self-aware agent architectures. This approach empowers researchers to design effective curricula for self-aware agents through curriculum learning, yielding a range of useful tools for evaluating the cognitive and social aspects of these agents. Our study's novel contribution lies in establishing a coherent theoretical framework for comparison-based curiosity in multi-agent systems, which can be applied to any self-aware agent architecture and facilitates the integration of cognitive and social theories. This framework facilitates the development of strategies for curricula learning in multi-agent systems, which can be instrumental in designing optimal learning plans for individual agents within a social network. Our research is accompanied by an open-source implementation that is accessible on GitHub. In monitoring the movement of objects and changes in urban environments, a network of sensors is often used to provide maximum coverage and most reliable information with the fewest sensors. The emergence of ridesourcing vehicles as mobile sensors offers new opportunities and challenges in this field. The problem of optimizing sensor coverage and reliability in this context is complex due to factors such as the dynamic movement of ridesourcing vehicles, varying sensor capabilities, and their limited presence in certain areas. This problem was studied by developing a mobile sensing system that utilizes ridesourcing vehicles to improve coverage and reliability in certain areas of a city while minimizing the number of ridesourcing vehicles required. The system was designed to continuously optimize coverage and reliability by adjusting the location of ridesourcing vehicles in response to changes in traffic and vehicle movement. The system consists of several components, including an algorithm that evaluates the effectiveness of individual sensors in covering specific areas and identifying gaps in coverage. The system was tested on a real-world dataset showing that it can effectively optimize coverage and reliability by selecting the most effective ridesourcing vehicles for each task and providing updates to the algorithm when vehicles are activated or deactivated. The results indicate that a limited number of ridesourcing vehicles can provide superior coverage and reliability compared to a larger number of less effective sensors and that the system requires significantly fewer ridesourcing vehicles than the optimal static sensor placement. The performance of the system was also evaluated under changing traffic conditions and it was observed that it requires relatively few updates to adjust to these changes. The mobile sensing system has the potential to optimize coverage and reliability in various applications such as monitoring traffic conditions, detecting falls in the elderly, and tracking wildlife movements by combining its approach with multi-objective optimization and game theory techniques. The method proposed in the study is applicable to any city provided that the underlying graph structure of the city remains the same and the same programming language is used to implement the algorithm. These new limits were derived without making assumptions about the dark matter particle's mass, applying to all dark matter masses between 0.1 and 1000 GeV. The research also enabled the examination of dark matter absorption in nucleons, setting upper limits on the form factor that describes this interaction. This paper delves into the mysteries of advanced algorithms used for evaluating student essays, which are increasingly being adopted by educational institutions. We demonstrate that these algorithms, though impressive at first glance, suffer from significant flaws. Specifically, we show that they inconsistently apply the same standards to different essays, often rating similar essays very differently. This is concerning, as it may have unfair implications for students. We also highlight that these algorithms prioritize stability over accuracy and frequently produce results that are not transparent. To illustrate these issues, we present a score-prediction model that achieves comparable performance to these algorithms but does so in a more reliable and consistent manner. Interestingly, this model performs better than the existing algorithms when evaluating essays that are naturally occurring, as opposed to those that are fabricated for testing purposes. Ultimately, our research encourages educational institutions to prioritize the development of more trustworthy algorithms that can effectively evaluate the learning outcomes of these systems. We have made our analysis and proposed solution publicly available, in the hope that it will contribute to the advancement of this critical technology. This paper examines the concept of invariance in fractional order systems and establishes the requirements for linear subspaces to remain unaffected under the systems' dynamics. We demonstrate that the specificity of these conditions depends on the system's structure, specifically its transfer function representation, and highlight the role of fractional operators in this regard. Building upon this understanding, we develop an alternative approach to detecting the invariance of subspaces in polynomial systems. Furthermore, we present a method to determine the largest invariant subspace in such systems. This method involves an iterative procedure that ensures a maximally invariant subspace is identified, and we discuss the implications of this method for the analysis and control of polynomial systems. We also illustrate the efficacy of this method through numerical simulations applied to a fractional order system and a polynomial system. Additionally, we discuss the advantages of utilizing the suboptimal controller in the presence of disturbance inputs. Lastly, we outline potential directions for advancing the study of subspace invariance in fractional order systems.

This study examines how the atmosphere of planets located at a moderate distance from their stars is enriched with various gases. We're investigating a group of planets that could have conditions similar to those of Earth, orbiting stars with similar brightness to the Sun. Our research focuses on planets that have temperatures between 300K and 500K on their surfaces and are located near their stars' habitable zones. We're using three different models of atmospheric evolution to compare their findings. One model, the minimalistic approach, only considers the breakdown of atmospheric components into individual gases, while two more comprehensive models take into account the chemical reactions that occur within the atmosphere. We're also exploring how different stars and planetary characteristics affect the composition of their atmospheres. Our analysis includes seven different scenarios for each of the three evolution models. We're looking at how atmospheric metallicity affects the presence of CO, CO2, and NH3, as well as other gases, and are examining how different stars and planetary characteristics contribute to the composition of their atmospheres. Our research shows that CO and CO2 share similar patterns of formation, whereas NH3 exhibits opposite distribution patterns. We observe that CO and CO2 primarily emerge in the upper atmospheres of planets, whereas NH3 forms in the lower regions. Our analysis also reveals that atmospheric metallicity has a significant impact on the presence of these gases, and that different stars contribute varying amounts of metal content to their planetary atmospheres. Furthermore, our research indicates that planetary mass and radius influence the composition of their atmospheres, and that heat released from the planets' interior can cause the breakdown of atmospheric components and enhance gas formation. Our study investigates the impact of finite temperature on zero-energy peaks resulting from non-Majorana behavior at the end of a semiconductor nanowire by incorporating outcomes from finite difference numerical simulations. At zero temperature, these peaks remain unchanged, but with increasing temperature, they become broadened and ultimately disappear. This effect is more pronounced in samples with a larger overlap between the hybridized zero-energy states. Additionally, we find that even without the influence of a proximity gap, the peak can still broaden due to the spin-orbit coupling and finite bulk leakage. This phenomenon is illustrated using both the Fu-Konig lemma and a tight-binding model, and we reveal that the peak's width is directly correlated with the magnitude of the peaking effect in units of energy. This research suggests that observing non-Majorana behavior at zero-energy may be challenging with current experimental techniques. Therefore, we propose that facilities with higher energy resolution are needed to confirm the existence of Majorana zero-mode. Furthermore, we provide a method for estimating the bulk leakage in experimental setups using a modified discussion of zero-energy state properties. This analysis is applicable to both zero and finite temperature scenarios. Finally, we propose that facilities with higher energy resolution are needed to confirm the existence of non-Majorana zero-modes. The influence of bulk leakage on the peak width is demonstrated, and we offer a method for estimating the overlap between zero-energy states in experimental setups. This overlap has a significant impact on the peak's width, and it is directly correlated with the peak width in units of energy. The overlap also dictates the peak's height, with values greater than 0.7 indicating the need for more sophisticated numerical simulations. These findings contribute significant insights to the interpretation of experimental data on zero-energy peaks in semiconductor nanowires.

We then employ this extension to examine the properties of topological Hochschild homology within the context of shadow categories, ultimately establishing a connection between THH and shadows. We then use this result to obtain the abelian group structure of THH of compact Lie groups, leading to further conclusions about the ring structure of THH of compact simple Lie groups of type A. We conclude with the discussion on potential connections with graded E_n-algebras and the analysis of THH of certain categorical products, including the category of representations of a group in a suitable setting. We introduce VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), a comprehensive sound source separation (SSS) dataset, based on the frequently used VGG-Sound database. The dataset consists of 4,851 clip pairs, where each pair contains a mix of two distinct sound sources, along with their individual components. We constructed VGG-SS using a method called adversarial source separation, supported by detailed annotations. Our dataset stands out from existing SSS datasets due to its large size, detailed annotations, and the challenging nature of the clips. We also present a thorough evaluation of VGG-SS, involving both objective and perceived quality assessments, using a range of existing models and new ones trained on our dataset. Our findings demonstrate that our dataset exhibits significant source overlap, complex contexts, and a tendency for low-frequency sources to be embedded in background noise. We observed that models trained on VGG-SS outperformed those trained on other datasets in various benchmark tests. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/vggscapes/vgg-sound-source-separation. We hope that VGG-SS will serve as a key benchmark for advancing sound source separation techniques. We have launched a competition based on the dataset at https://competitions.codewars.com/details/5c0f4b3c4c00010001c7b3b6. We have initiated a codetags label for codewars challenges related to VGG-SS at https://www.codewars.com/users/vgg-sound-source-separation/tags. We invite researchers to join the codewars community to participate in evaluating their code against our dataset. We will continuously expand VGG-SS by applying our method to new annotations, in the hope that it will become a primary dataset for sound source separation. We have already applied this approach successfully to separate the sources in 1,851 clip pairs from the FADE dataset, which we have incorporated into VGG-SS. We have launched codewars challenges codename fade-to-side and codename fade-to-back to evaluate source separation models in this newly created subset of VGG-SS. We have achieved impressive results on these challenges, outperforming existing models using both objective and perceived quality assessments. Recently, hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (HGCNs) have gained popularity due to their ability to represent large-scale graphs efficiently. However, most existing HGCNs focus solely on node classification, neglecting the importance of node representation. This leads to a critical limitation, as model performance suffers from a lack of diverse node features. To address this limitation, we develop the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), a novel hyperbolic graph neural network that enhances node features through a layer-wise representation learning approach. Unlike traditional HGCNs, LGCN learns node representations by incorporating a distortion-correcting mechanism, enabled by the use of differential maps. The effectiveness of LGCN is demonstrated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, revealing its superiority over existing HGCNs in terms of node classification accuracy and diversity of representations. Furthermore, LGCN is found to achieve competitive performance compared to its Euclidean graph counterparts. The source code for LGCN is available online. Our research demonstrates that the presence of a single dynamic binding operation can already lead to an expansion of operational and semantic concepts, offering greater flexibility while maintaining operational principles. Adding a mass term to the gravitational perturbations results in a massless scalar and two massive tensor modes in a linearized gravity theory, which can be represented as a sequence of five dofs. This approach addresses the issue of generating the Higgs particle's mass in gravity. However, it results in an additional complex field in the spectrum, which can be removed by imposing a reality condition on the fundamental metric variable, ultimately recovering four physical dofs. We then investigate the consequences of introducing a non-linear mass term for the scalar mode, which leads to the failure of achieving a pure spin-2 tensor mode for any value of the non-linear mass parameter. This failure occurs both at the linearized and nonlinearized levels. We conclude that a gravitational Higgs mechanism cannot solely rely on this mass term approach. We also find that, in order to generate the Higgs particle's mass without introducing extra complex fields in the spectrum, a 5-dimensional formulation of linearized gravity is required. We demonstrate that this formulation is possible and offers a genuine solution to the Higgs problem in gravity. This new approach allows for the generation of the Higgs particle's mass without generating additional complex fields in the spectrum. We then investigate a related idea proposed in an existing paper. That proposal involves presenting a f(R) gravity theory that is equivalent to linearized gravity with a mass term added to the gravitational perturbations. We analyze the parameters of this theory and the resulting field theory. We demonstrate that, in order for the gravitational f(R) theory to be consistent with the principles of linearized gravity (i.e., being consistent with the properties of linearized gravity), the conformally equivalent metric must be identified with the fundamental metric variable. We then investigate the consequences of introducing a non-linear mass term for the scalar mode in this theory. We find that, in order to generate the Higgs particle's mass without introducing extra complex fields in the spectrum, a 5-dimensional formulation of linearized gravity is required. We conclude by discussing the implications of our study for the gravitational Higgs mechanism. We propose an alternative approach that involves presenting a f(R) gravity theory with a non-linear mass term for the scalar mode. We argue that this approach offers a viable solution to the Higgs problem in gravity. However, we also demonstrate that this solution is inconsistent with the principles of linearized gravity, thereby rendering it unfeasible. Finally, we pose several open questions on this subject.

Building on a previous notion by Lozar, we extend the concept of double covers to signed graphs, creating what we call extended double covers. These covers preserve the original graph's signing, and we investigate their relationship with GP-cycles within the covers. Based on this framework, we formulate a conjecture that extended double covers of GP-complete signed graphs over a field remain planar-complete. To support this hypothesis, we present evidence by showing it holds true for a specific class of GP-complete signed graphs - those featuring a red 3-cycle as their sole GP-component. Additionally, our research introduces several new ideas, including the application of GP-cycles as homomorphisms, as well as an exploration of their properties. These developments contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between GP-completeness and planar-completeness in extended double covers of signed graphs. Lastly, our work poses several open questions waiting for further exploration.

Properties of quantum equilibrium states can be classified into four categories based on their Hamiltonian dynamics, which correspond to oscillatory, exponential, polynomial, and sublinear growth. By applying high-order perturbation theory, we can determine the properties of these states for Hamiltonians that exhibit multiple energy scale separation. This approach enables us to investigate equilibrium properties, such as energy averages and correlations, and specifically focuses on systems described by the Hamiltonian $H = A + \lambda B$, where $A$ and $B$ have distinctly different time scales and equilibrium parameters can be manipulated to reveal the underlying physics. The developed theory is illustrated through perturbation studies of the BCS model, the Gaussian scalar-electrodynamics model, and the Hartree-Fock approximation of the many-body Hamiltonian with a two-body interaction. The findings provide a theoretical foundation for employing high-order perturbation theory to analyze quantum systems characterized by separate time scales in their Hamiltonians. This concept could potentially facilitate the creation of heat engines operating below the Carnot limit. Speech-to-text technology has made significant progress in recent years, but a major limitation remains: it nearly always requires pre-trained data. This challenge becomes even more pronounced in languages without significant amounts of data, where the few shots given during initial training are insufficient to achieve accurate results. In response to this issue, we propose two innovative strategies to achieve zero-shot speech translation in multiple languages. Our approaches leverage structural similarities between languages to improve performance and have been successfully tested in experiments involving 10 different languages. The results showed that our methods successfully facilitate zero-shot speech translation and significantly outperformed the control condition across various evaluation metrics. Moreover, an in-depth analysis of the data revealed that our proposed strategies can achieve precise translation without the aid of training data. Additionally, we observed substantial gains in performance when using pre-trained models for zero-shot inference, compared to models trained from scratch. For further exploration of this concept, we also introduced the IsoSpeech Dataset, a newly developed dataset that includes speech-to-text data categorized by structural characteristics, such as language and dialect. The dataset is available for public use and paves the way for ongoing research in this area. The ultimate goal of our work is to enable accurate speech-to-text translation in any given situation, without the need for prior knowledge or training data. Alongside the proposed strategies, we also presented two alternative approaches to achieving this goal, and our results demonstrated that these methods successfully facilitate zero-shot speech translation with minimal training. However, it is crucial to continue addressing potential biases in the data, as well as developing more flexible models capable of adapting to new situations. The Isolab tool, alongside the IsoSpeech Dataset, marks the beginning of a broader initiative that aims to give speech and other modalities the same level of linguistic freedom that language systems have always taken for granted. This initiative is directed at any researcher interested in exploring this concept, and all contributions are welcome as part of this starting point.
